terms.definition: The result folders, shortened to their number after first use: 001 is run 1, 002 run 2, 003 the control run, 004 run 3, 007 boot C, 010 boot E, 011 boot F1.
The Arm clean-and-invalidate-by-address instruction. The harness runs it on every line of a chain before a flushed timed pass.
A latency result where every line of the chain was cleaned and invalidated with DC CIVAC before one timed pass.
A random pointer chain walked once and never flushed. Since run 2 the fresh chains supply the SLC value.
The average time of one dependent load in the pointer chain, in nanoseconds.
The lowest value of three repeated passes over the same chain. Run 1's flushed rows used this method.
System level cache, the cache in the CMN mesh (Arm's coherent mesh interconnect). 3.75 MiB of it caches DRAM (5 home nodes x 1 MiB, 4 of 16 ways locked as OCM).
On-chip memory, held in locked ways of the SLC. OCM rows were not affected by this defect.
The core caches. DSU is Arm's DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds the L3. The flush was meant to clear only these.
A counter: how many lines a cache fetched from the next level per timed load. A value of 1.00 means every load missed that cache.

The run 2 harness options for the flushed 8 MiB row (fresh=3). Run 1 had used --flush --reps 3 (fresh=0), a chain already walked twice in warm-up [001 and 002 latency-dram-flushed.csv:1, run_asimov.sh:24 to :32, :115].

Over all nine single reps the range was 18.8 to 26.0 ns per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]
The flush was DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction, which pushes lines out of the core caches). [001 README.md line 36]

The flushed DRAM rows of 1 to 8 MiB in run 1 read 52.7 ns per load, the DRAM value (best rows 52.716, 52.714, 52.713, 52.711 ns). [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]

The OCM rows stayed at 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
The open question was how the OCM lock is set up. [run1-report.html line 491]
A plain locked range (set by the registers hnf_slc_lock_ways and lock_base) and the CMN OCM mode (a mode of the Arm CMN S3 mesh) behave differently on a flush. [run1-report.html line 491]
The Arm CMN S3 TRM (Technical Reference Manual) says a CleanInvalid of an OCM-mode line does nothing in the SLC. [run1-report.html line 491]
It also says a locked line in a normal range can be pushed to memory by a non-allocating request. [run1-report.html line 491]
No memory sits behind OCM. If the flush had removed the OCM lines from the SLC, the data would have had nowhere to come back from. [README.md lines 40 to 46, run1-report.html line 491]
Run 1 showed that the data stayed. So the question was about interpretation and not about safety. [README.md lines 40 to 46, run1-report.html line 491]

chart.title: Run 1 flushed rows: OCM regions stay near 20 ns, DRAM reads 52.7 ns
chart.takeaway: The same DC CIVAC flush sent DRAM-backed loads to 52.7 ns per load. Every OCM row stayed at 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load. OCM lines stay in the SLC in CMN OCM mode.

terms.definition: On-chip memory: 4 locked SLC ways in each home node, 256 KiB per region, five regions (OCM0 to OCM4), with no memory behind it.
System level cache: the cache held in the CMN home nodes.
A CMN mesh node that owns a slice of the address space and holds its SLC lines. Asimov has five, with CMN node ids 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344 for OCM0 to OCM4.
The Arm Coherent Mesh Network, version S3: the mesh that connects the clusters, the home nodes and memory.

A CMN setting (HN_CFG_CTL bit HN_OCM_EN) where a home node keeps a locked range in the SLC and never sends requests for it to memory. A CleanInvalid or CleanShared of such a line ends in the SLC and does not invalidate the line.
A normal SLC range held by the hnf_slc_lock_ways and lock_base registers. A locked line in such a range can be pushed to memory by a non-allocating request.
The Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction. It pushes a line out of the core caches. The pages call rows that use it "flushed" rows.
The CMN mesh transactions that a core flush becomes when it reaches a home node.
Nanoseconds per dependent load in a pointer chain. Lower is faster.
Each latency row was run several times (reps). The best row is the fastest rep.
A pointer chain that has never been walked before the timed walk (the --fresh option), so no earlier walk could have warmed a cache.
DynamIQ Shared Unit: a 2-core cluster. The L2 and L3 are shared by the two cores of a DSU.
The count of L3 read refills divided by the number of loads. A value of 1.00 means every load left the DSU.
cmncount reads the CMN mesh counters. hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all counts the requests a home node received.
The System Control Processor firmware that programs the mesh at boot. program_ocm in asimov_physical_sam.c sets the OCM registers.
Technical Reference Manual: the Arm document for the CMN S3. It is not in refs/.
The result folders of run 1 (ran 2026-10-31) and run 2 (ran 2026-11-02). The bracket citations shorten them to 001 and 002.

polished.one_line: Run 1's OCM write row at 7.2 GB/s timed the cache flush rather than the stores. The fixed row reads 20.4 GB/s.
looked_wrong: One core (CPU 2) wrote OCM1 (OCM is the on-chip memory, and region 1 is 256 KiB) in one pass with --flush-after. The row read 7.18 GB/s in run 1 [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, log.txt:29].
The same core copied OCM1 to OCM2 (256 KiB, --flush-before and --flush-after) at 11.96 GB/s in run 1 [001 bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:7, log.txt:30].
Four cores writing one OCM region each read 29.2 GB/s in total, 7.2 to 7.4 GB/s per core, in run 1 [001 bandwidth-ocm-4core.csv:11-14].
The same core writes DRAM at 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s at every footprint from 16 KiB to 32 MiB in run 1 [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86].
The write row took 36.5 to 36.6 us (262,144 bytes at 7.16 to 7.18 GB/s). 256 KiB of stores at 32 GB/s take 8.2 us [001 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-6].
The copy row took 43.8 us (524,288 bytes at 11.965 GB/s) [001 bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:5].
why_wrong: The expectation was a store rate near the core's 32 GB/s DRAM write rate from run 1 [run1-report.html section 5a].
Instead, with --flush-after the timed span held the 256 KiB of stores plus one DC CIVAC (clean and invalidate by address) for each of the 4,096 lines [bandwidth.c:248-254, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 77-81].
The stores take 8.2 us at 32 GB/s. The remaining 28.3 us is the flush, about 6.9 ns per line (est., run 1) [run1-report.html section 5a].
So 7.2 GB/s is the rate of stores into the core caches plus a serial write-back to OCM, not a streaming OCM write rate [run1-report.html section 5a].
The copy row's 43.8 us is about 16 us of loads from OCM1 plus about 28 us of flush of OCM2 (est., run 1). The 4-core write row has the same defect [run1-report.html section 5a].
A 256 KiB buffer also fits in L2 plus L3 (384 KiB in total). The lines never leave the cluster during the timed pass [run1-report.html section 5a, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127].
Jesse's README lists three OCM row kinds timed without a flush first. Its own rule says every timed OCM pass starts flushed [001 README.md line 35].

tests.name: Streaming OCM write, one core, 1.25 MiB over five regions, flush before
tests.run: run 2, control run, run 3, boot F1
tests.measures: Measures the one-core OCM write rate with the flush outside the timed span (bandwidth --threads 1 --cpus 2 --mem ocm --ocm-regions 0,1,2,3,4 --bytes 1280K --kernel write --flush-before --passes 8 --reps 3). The 1.25 MiB buffer is 3.3 times the 384 KiB of L2 plus L3. Lines then reach OCM by eviction. The flawed write, copy and 4-core rows were dropped. A rate near 32 GB/s would mean run 1 timed only the flush. A lower rate would mean one core writes OCM slower than it writes DRAM [002 log.txt:59, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127 and 228-232].

tests.measures: Measures whether the CME's (the cluster's streaming unit that issues loads and stores for the cores) store path reaches a higher OCM write rate than the core's, with the same command plus --cme. A higher CME rate would mean the core's 20.3 GB/s is not a limit of OCM itself [004 log.txt:117, CME-plan.md line 102, test 7].

tests.name: Both OCM write rows with the L3 on, then prefetchers off
tests.measures: Measures whether the L3 (run 3's command set rerun on the L3-on firmware) or the data prefetchers (turned off in boot F2) change the core's or the CME's OCM write rate. A changed rate would mean that unit takes part in the write path [011 and 012 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].

showed: Run 2: one core writes OCM at 20.3 to 20.4 GB/s over three reps, best 20.433 GB/s. This is the first row free of the flush defect [002 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-7].
Jesse noted it sits below one core's 32.0 GB/s store rate to DRAM [002 README.md line 86].
The run 1 write-then-flush row, the copy row and the 4-core OCM write row were dropped from run 2 onward [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 107 and 228-232].
run1-report.html section 5a proposed 4 passes. The plan and the run used 8 [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 107 and 228-232, 002 log.txt:59].

Control run (run 2's code on run 1's firmware): 20.338 GB/s. Run 3: core 20.326 GB/s, CME 19.795 GB/s [003 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, 004 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, 004 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].
In run 3 the CME writes DRAM at 62.0 to 63.9 GB/s at every footprint from 16 KiB to 32 MiB [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86,101,116].
In run 3 the core writes DRAM at 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s. So both write OCM slower than they write DRAM [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11-86].
Boot F1 (L3 on): the core's OCM write stays at 20.326 GB/s, unchanged to three decimals from run 3 [011 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].
Boot F1: the CME's OCM write rises to 30.659 GB/s by the bracket and 30.977 GB/s in span, 1.549 times run 3 [011 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, README.md line 317, asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.6].
Boot F2 (prefetchers off): CME 30.994 GB/s by the bracket, 31.327 GB/s in span [012 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, README.md line 133].
polished.open: Why one core's OCM streaming write sits at 20.3 GB/s (run 2 through boot F1), below its 32.0 GB/s DRAM store rate, is not explained in any primary file. The OCM and DRAM write rows differ in page size (OCM in 4 KiB pages, DRAM in 2 MiB pages). They also differ in flush state (OCM flushed once before its 8 passes per rep, DRAM never flushed). A run that changes one of these at a time would settle which one matters [004 README.md line 84, CSV header lines].

terms.definition: On-chip memory, used here as five regions (OCM0 to OCM4) of 256 KiB each.
Short for the result folders membench-jibin-001 and so on: run 1, run 2, the control run, run 3, boot F1 and boot F2.
The cluster's streaming unit that issues loads and stores for the cores. The harness selects it with --cme.
The clean-and-invalidate-by-address instruction that writes one cache line back and drops it from the cache.
Harness flags: run the DC CIVAC flush of the buffer after the timed pass (inside the timed span in run 1) or before it (outside the timed span).
The two cache levels of one cluster, 128 KiB plus 256 KiB, 384 KiB in total.
A pass is one sweep of the kernel over the buffer. A rep is one timed group of passes, and the CSV lists each rep and the best.
Two rates for a CME row: by the bracket is from the timer around the whole call, in span is from the timer inside the call.
Run 2's harness code run on run 1's firmware (membench-jibin-003), to separate code changes from firmware changes.
Run 6 boots on the L3-on firmware. F2 also has the data prefetchers turned off.
The buffer size a bandwidth row sweeps, here 16 KiB to 32 MiB.
An estimate computed from other measured numbers, not a direct measurement.

polished.one_line: 256 KiB flushed chains counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills per load, below the 1.00 a dependent chain should need.
looked_wrong: Run 1: every 256 KiB flushed row (five OCM region rows and one DRAM row) counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]
The same rows counted 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills (event 0x17) per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]
Run 1 rows of 1 MiB and more counted 1.00 of each.
DRAM flushed 1 to 8 MiB read 1.0001 to 1.0012 refills per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
OCM all-five flushed 1.25 MiB read 1.0004 to 1.0012 refills per load. [001 latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]
The run 1 DRAM 256 KiB row got faster as its L3 count fell.
It read 44.698, 39.031 and 35.689 ns per load at 0.9043, 0.8459 and 0.7839 L3 read refills per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv reps 0 to 2]
Run 2 fresh chains (never walked before the timed pass) did not change it.
Run 2's 40 passes on 20 per-region rows counted 0.76 to 0.95 L3 and 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load. [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 002 README line 66]
In 19 of 20 rows the faster pass had fewer L3 read refills. [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 002 README line 66]
Run 3 sparse chains (one member line per 4 KiB page) counted 1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills per load over 140 passes. [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 004 README line 111]
The same passes counted 0.47 to 1.14 L3 read refills per load. [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 004 README line 111]
why_wrong: A dependent chain (each load's address comes from the previous load) asks for one cache line per load. So each cache level should show at most 1.00 refills per load.
Fewer than 1.00 L3 read refills per load means 9 to 23 % of the lines (1 minus 0.91, 1 minus 0.77) were already inside the cluster when the load asked for them.
More than 1.00 L2 refills per load means the L2 filled lines the chain never asked for.
The run 1 to run 3 counter set (0x03 L1 refills, 0x17 L2 refills, 0xA2 L3 read refills) counts fills by level, not by cause. [common.h line 336]
So a hardware prefetcher was a hypothesis, not a measurement, until run 4.
On runs 1 to 3 and on boots A and B the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data (snoop-filter-only mode). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]
So an L3 read refill on these rows means a demand read that left the cluster. The early-arriving lines sat in the L2. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]

tests.name: Fresh chains with flush on every per-region OCM row
tests.measures: Each timed pass walks a chain never walked before (CSV header fresh=3 flush=1, two timed passes per row, fresh1 and fresh2). A count that stays below 1.00 L3 read refills per load would mean an unseen chain does not remove the early-arriving lines. [002, commit 8ae533c, 2026-11-02]

tests.name: Sparse chains (one member per 4 KiB page) plus dense all-five control
tests.measures: Per-region latency when no neighbouring line is a chain member (chain c uses line 8c+4 of every page, 7 timed passes of 64 loads per region). The dense all-five control row (run 2's all-five arguments) checks that the platform repeats run 2. [004, commit ba834c0, 2026-11-03, latency.c lines 21 to 22]

tests.name: Prefetch refill events on every OCM row plus sequential 8 MiB chain
tests.measures: How many fills per load each prefetcher made, using events 0x81BC (L1D refills requested by a hardware prefetcher), 0x81BD (L2 refills by prefetchers targeting the L2) and 0x0111 (L2 refills from the L1D prefetcher's requests). terms.definition: A pointer-chasing test where each load's address comes from the previous load, so the chain asks for one cache line per load.

A chain never walked before the timed pass (--fresh 3), so no earlier walk could have left its lines in a cache.
The default chain shape, as against sparse. Run 3 added the sparse shape, and rows from earlier runs are dense.
A chain with one member line per 4 KiB page (line 8c+4 of every page for chain c), so no neighbouring line is a member.

One chain that spans all five OCM regions. Its dense form is the OCM number the pages quote.
A performance counter event that counts lines filled into the L2, by any cause.
A performance counter event that counts demand reads that left the cluster. It does not count prefetch fills.
A counter value divided by the number of loads in the pass. A dependent chain should show at most 1.00 at each level.
A unit inside the core that fetches lines the program has not asked for yet, guessing from the address pattern.
L2 refills made by prefetchers targeting the L2.
L1D refills requested by a hardware prefetcher, and L2 refills from the L1D prefetcher's requests.
An L3 setting under which the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data.
The group of cores that share one L3. An L3 read refill counts a demand read that left this group.

Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware. Build 0.35.0-pfoff.1 turns the data prefetchers off at every core power-on.
IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28, the register bits that disable the core and CME data prefetchers.
A row is one test configuration. A pass is one timed walk of the chain (64 loads on the OCM rows). Run 1 calls a pass a rep. A row mean averages its timed passes.

terms.definition: On-chip memory. It has five regions, OCM0 to OCM4, at 1, 3 or 5 crosspoints from a core.
A chain of dependent loads, one per 64-byte line. Each load's address comes from the previous load, so the time per load is the memory latency.
A chase that starts after the caches were cleaned, so the first pass should miss on every line.
A chain built new for each pass (run 2), so no earlier pass could have left its lines in a cache.
A chase with one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads a pass, best of 7 passes (run 3). Every load should be a demand miss to a flushed line.
A chase that touches every line of the region. The dense all-five row covers all five OCM regions.
The other team's benchmark. Its OCM1 number is 14.42 ns per load for a 64 KiB (16-page) chase after DC CIVAC.
The Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction. It removes a line from the caches before the chase starts.
A core counter: how many lines the cluster L3 fetched from outside per chase load. A value of 1.0 means one home-node read per load. A value below 1.0 means some lines were already in the cluster.
A core counter: how many lines the cluster L2 fetched per chase load. A value above 1.0 means extra lines were fetched, most likely by hardware prefetch.
One switch on the CMN mesh. The distance from a core to an OCM region is counted in crosspoints (1, 3 or 5 here).
The mesh node that owns an address range and answers reads of it from outside the cluster.
System level cache, at the home node. asimov-bench read one SLC line in 20.0 ns on a waveform.
The Arm mesh interconnect that joins the clusters to the home nodes.
The core's 16-entry translation cache for data addresses. A 16-page set fits it, a 64-page region does not.
A page-table setting (boots C and D) that maps OCM in 64 KiB units, so one TLB entry covers 16 pages.
Core logic that fetches lines before a load asks for them. Boot B turns the data prefetchers off.
Separate boots, each with a different setting: A is the baseline, B prefetchers off, C and D 64 KiB translations, E and F1 the DSU L3 on for CPUs 2 to 9.
The cluster-level cache in the DSU (the Arm DynamIQ Shared Unit), shared by the cores of a cluster. The stock SCP enables the full L3 for cluster 0 only.
The system control processor firmware. It decides which clusters have their L3 enabled at boot.
The hardware design source (register transfer level). asimov-bench's number is from RTL 6da3026.
Boot B rows that record the mesh path (X steps and Y steps) for each OCM region, used for the distance fit.
The n-th root of the product of n ratios. 0.950 times boot A means the rows are 5 % faster on average.
Root mean square error of the fit. 0.09 ns rms means the fit misses the 20 cells by 0.09 ns on average.

terms.definition: A test where each load's address comes from the previous load, so loads cannot overlap and the time per load is the full memory latency.
A chain whose cache lines were evicted with DC CIVAC before the walk, so every load misses the caches.
The Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction that writes a cache line back and removes it from the caches.
The same chain walked in increasing address order instead of random order, used to see whether the memory serves neighbouring addresses faster.
A node on the mesh that handles memory requests for its part of the address space and holds the SLC. The 2 MiB chain measures the core-to-home-node round trip.
System level cache, the cache held at the home nodes of the mesh. A 2 MiB chain fits in it and measures the core-to-home-node round trip alone.
Arm's coherent mesh network, which connects the cores, the home nodes and the memory ports.
Hardware in the core that fetches cache lines before the core asks for them. Counters 0x81BC and 0x81BD count its refills.
A load the core itself requested that missed in every cache, as opposed to a line a prefetcher brought in early.
A cache line brought into the L3 by a read miss. A count of 1.0 per load means every load missed the L3.
Trusted Firmware-A, the Arm boot firmware. A hook in it set bit 48 of IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 to turn the data prefetchers off.
The core's extended control register. Bit 48 disables the data prefetchers.
The low-power DRAM type a real chip would use. A random read costs about 50 ns est. inside the chip alone.
The time a DRAM bank needs to open a row, read it and close it (precharge, activate, column access).
Real DRAM serves addresses in the same open row faster than random addresses. A memory with no row behaviour serves both at the same speed.
The Arm reference board used for comparison: a Neoverse V3AE core at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-8000 memory.
The earlier Asimov benchmark whose DRAM chase numbers (31.65 ns and 53.3 ns per load) run 1 was compared with.
The memory asimov-bench's chases ran against, as run 1's README names it: a model, not DRAM chips.
The hardware design source (register-transfer level) that the emulator image is built from. Named by a commit hash such as asimov-rtl 0d9e214eb43b.
The main memory of the AP (application processor) cores, the memory the chains walk.
A simulated memory block that answers AXI bus reads and writes with configurable delays. Four of them are used as the AP DRAM, one per SMS lane.
One of the four memory ports (XMS lanes 32-35) behind which one memory model sits.
The mesh node that forwards memory requests from the mesh to a memory port.
The block that converts the mesh's CHI protocol requests into AXI bus requests for the memory model.
A test run in the Cadence Xcelium simulator in the repo, not on the emulator. The 3 ns model response was checked only there.
The emulator build that the Asimov runs execute on. The model's 3 ns response has not been checked on it.
An estimate or a derived value, not a direct measurement.

terms.definition: On-chip memory. SRAM that software addresses directly. It is 4 of the 16 SLC ways in each home node, locked by the firmware.
System level cache. The cache array in each mesh home node. The 2 MiB DRAM-backed chain fits in it, so its loads are SLC hits.
A node on the mesh that holds one SLC array. There are five.
One switch point on the mesh. A CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes is the mean of |dx|+|dy| in crosspoints from its cluster port.
One 1.25 MiB pointer chain that runs over all five 256 KiB OCM regions. Each load in the chain depends on the previous one.
Two forms of the all-five chain on run 3. The dense row is the control. The sparse row touches one line per 4 KiB page.
Two conditions of the run 1 all-five row, reported in separate files (latency-ocm-all5-fresh.csv and latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv).
A 2 MiB DRAM-backed pointer chain on 2 MiB huge pages. It sits in the SLC and is the comparison row for an SLC hit.
The count of cache line fills at L1, L2 or L3 per chain load. A value of 1.00 at every level means each load missed all three levels and was served by a home node.
Translation lookaside buffer. The core's cache of page translations. A chain on 4 KiB pages can miss it where a chain on 2 MiB huge pages does not.
The kernel device that maps an OCM region into a process. It maps in 4 KiB pages.
The OCM page setting on boots C and D. The OCM is mapped in 64 KiB translation entries instead of 4 KiB pages.
The DSU L3 holds data. This is the setting on boot E and boot F1.
DynamIQ Shared Unit. The cluster unit that holds the L3.
The lowest-latency row in a result CSV file. Every number quoted here is a row best.
Nanoseconds for one dependent pointer load in the chain.

The two 2 MiB passes on run 1 differ by only 0.14 ns. The 3 MiB step is about 10 times that repeat spread.
The 4 MiB chain read 29.760 ns per load on run 1. [001 latency-dram-large.csv:22, :30, :46]
That is 20.4 % of the way from the 2 MiB SLC row (23.980 ns) to the 32 MiB DRAM row (52.300 ns).

Its bests on the runs are 29.760 ns per load (run 1), 28.704 (run 2), 28.399 (control run) and 28.270 (run 3). [latency-dram-large.csv of 001 to 011]

The 8 MiB fresh chain read 45.077 ns per load on run 3. The 8 MiB flushed chain (the same chain walked after a cache flush) read 52.738 ns per load on run 3. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39, 004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7]
The 32 MiB fresh chain read 52.185 ns on run 3. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:47]

At 4 MiB, 3.75/4 of the loads would hit. The prediction there is 25.8 ns per load est.
The measured 25.449 and 29.760 ns on run 1 are both higher. [computed from 001 latency-dram-large.csv:22, :46]
The transition is spread over 2 to 16 MiB instead of ending near 3.75 MiB.
Under an ideal-LRU model (LRU, least recently used: the cache evicts the line unused for longest), effective capacity = size x (1 - (lat - 23.980) / (52.300 - 23.980)).
The 3, 4, 6, 8 and 16 MiB points on run 1 then imply 2.84, 3.18, 2.64, 2.04 and 0.88 MiB est. of SLC, not one size. [recomputed from 001 latency-dram-large.csv:26, :30, :34, :38, :42]

terms.definition: System level cache: the shared cache held at the mesh home nodes. Jesse gives 3.75 MiB of SLC for DRAM as an RTL configuration figure (RTL, register transfer level: the hardware design source). The sweep does not measure the size itself.
A pointer chain walked right after it is written, with no cache flush before the walk.
The same pointer chain walked after the caches are flushed, so every load is expected to come from DRAM.
A chase walks a pointer chain with one dependent load per step. Latency is reported as nanoseconds per load.
Each chain is walked more than once. Each walk is a pass, and the best is the lowest pass.
One of the five mesh nodes that hold the SLC and answer memory requests.
One mesh step between a core and a home node. Mean distance to the five home nodes is given in crosspoints.
The DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, the Arm cluster block) L3 is the cluster-level cache. It was off on runs 001 to 008 and on for boot F1.
A core counter of cache lines fetched by the hardware prefetcher, divided by the chain loads. 0.0000 on boots A and B.
A core counter of lines brought into the L3 on reads, divided by the chain loads. 1.00 on both 8 MiB rows, so it cannot show SLC hits.
A cache model where the line unused for longest is evicted, so a chain larger than the cache hits for exactly cache-size / chain-size of its loads.
Run 003: run 1 firmware with run 2 code, used to separate firmware changes from code changes.
The mesh performance counters, used here to count requests at the five home nodes.
Result sets 005 (A), 006 (B, prefetchers off), 007 (C), 008 (D), 010 (E) and 011 (F1, L3 on). Runs 1, 2, control and 3 are 001, 002, 003 and 004.

On run 3 the 192 / 256 / 384 KiB chases read 14.045 / 19.333 / 22.729 ns per load [004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 53, 58, 63].
These values climb from the L2 level (6.090 ns per load at 128 KiB, run 3) [004 latency-dram-small.csv row 48].
They climb up to the SLC level (24.096 ns per load at 2 MiB, run 3), with no flat step between [004 latency-dram-large.csv row 23].
At 192 KiB on run 3 the best rep counted 0.5808 L2 refills and 0.4605 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-dram-small.csv row 50].
So 42 % of loads hit the L2, 46 % reached the mesh, and about 12 % (0.5808 minus 0.4605) were served by the L3.
On run 3 one core read a 256 KiB stream at 10.164 GB/s [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 52].
That is below the 14.817 to 16.619 GB/s of a 256 KiB OCM (on-chip memory on the mesh) region [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv row 7].
Jibin: 'L3 should be faster than OCM' [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:202].
Bill: 'L3 is confusing. 42% L2 hit rate?' [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:219].
why_wrong: Each DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, the two-core cluster) has a 256 KiB L3 beside its 128 KiB L2 [004 README.md:34].
A 192 KiB chain fits inside the L3.
The chase was therefore expected to read at one flat time between the L2 level (6.090 ns per load) and the SLC level (24.096 ns per load).
Instead it read 14.045 ns per load, with 46 % of loads leaving the cluster.
The L3 sits inside the cluster and OCM sits across the mesh.
So a 256 KiB read served by the L3 was expected to exceed the 14.817 to 16.619 GB/s OCM read on run 3, not fall below it at 10.164 GB/s.
First hypothesis (plan section 10, 2026-11-04): part of the 256 KiB L3 was powered down, the DSU's HALF RAM operating mode [follow-up-run-plan.md:191].

tests.name: L3 hit set: L2 hit, L3 read, L3 hit PMU events
tests.run: boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Counts L2 read hits, L3 read accesses and L3 read hits per load on the 64 to 512 KiB rows, instead of inferring them from refills. The PMU events are 0x81C5 L2D_CACHE_HIT_RD, 0xA0 L3D_CACHE_RD and 0x81C6 L3D_CACHE_HIT_RD, added in commit 7921962. 0x2A L3D_CACHE_REFILL is not implemented on the C1-Nano. A nonzero L3 hit count would mean the L3 holds data. 0.0000 would mean it holds none [follow-up-run-plan.md:191, 006 README.md:36].

terms.definition: A test that follows a chain of dependent loads, one per cache line, so the time per load is the latency of the level that holds the chain.
DynamIQ Shared Unit, the two-core cluster that holds the shared L2 (128 KiB) and L3 (256 KiB).
The second and third cache levels inside the cluster, 128 KiB and 256 KiB per DSU.
System-level cache, held by the home nodes on the mesh, outside the cluster.
On-chip memory, a region held by the home nodes on the mesh and read across the mesh.

Performance monitoring unit, the per-core hardware event counters (refills, hits, accesses) read per load.
A cache miss that brings a line into that cache, counted per load by the PMU.
The PMU event set (L2 read hit, L3 read, L3 read hit) added on boot B to count L3 hits directly.
The repetition of a row with the lowest time per load. It is the quoted row.
A cluster power-status register that reports the L3 slice count and L3 RAM state (0x0 = one slice, snoop-filter-only, 0x70 = all slices, FULL_ON).
An L3 RAM state in which the L3 keeps only its coherence directory and holds no data.

The Arm trusted firmware stage that powers cores on and, from boot B onward, prints the cluster state.
The power policy unit of a cluster and its power-request register, written by the SCP to stage an operating mode.
The matrix extension unit (Arm C1-SME2) attached to each DSU. F1 and F2 read the register around its hit-set row.
A separate pre-silicon latency benchmark whose 15.16 ns per load at 192 KiB is quoted as its L3 lower bound.

tests.name: 32 KiB and 192 KiB rows with prefetch refill counters
tests.run: boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Measures L1 refills per load on the 32 KiB row (the L1 edge), and the L1 prefetcher's share of them. Measures L1 refills per load on the 192 KiB row with the prefetchers on (A, C, E), off (B, D) and with the L3 on (E). A 192 KiB row that stays near 1.0 refills per load on every boot means the 100 % miss rate is the chain's construction. It is then not a prefetcher or measurement effect. Counters used: l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_load [005, 006, 007, 008, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28 and 50-53].

showed: The chain is one random cycle over all its lines. The test source builds it with Sattolo's algorithm, which yields a single cycle [latency.c lines 5-6] [transcript-peer.txt lines 1045-1054].
At 192 KiB the chain has 3,072 lines of 64 bytes, and the L1 holds 512 lines [004 latency-dram-small.csv header rows 24 and 49].
Each line is revisited only after 3,071 other loads. So every load misses the L1, whatever the step size.
The 100 % miss rate is the chain's construction, not a measurement defect.
The 192 KiB row reads 0.9986 to 0.9991 L1 refills per load on every boot A to E [005, 006, 007, 008, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-53].
This includes boot B with the prefetchers off (14.457 ns per load) and boot E with the L3 on (7.821 ns per load).
Run 3 read 14.045 ns per load on the same row [004 row 53].
The 32 KiB row repeats on every boot. With the prefetchers on (boots A, C, E) it reads 2.114, 2.117 and 2.121 ns per load [005, 007, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
On those boots it shows 0.0398 to 0.0447 L1 refills per load, 0.0078 to 0.0087 of them from the L1 prefetcher [005, 007, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
With the prefetchers off (boots B, D) the 32 KiB row reads 2.031 and 2.036 ns per load [006, 008 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
On those boots it shows 0.0094 to 0.0112 L1 refills per load and 0.0000 prefetch refills [006, 008 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
The peer session's reading of the 32 KiB row is a hypothesis, not a measurement [transcript-peer.txt line 1054].
In that reading, the kernel's own lines and the chain compete for the L1. Then 0.04 refills per load marks the L1 edge [transcript-peer.txt line 1054].
The current core page labels the 32 KiB row 'L1 and L2' in its Reads-from column [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1].
At boot E that row reads 2.121 ns per load and 0.04 L1 refills per load [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1].
polished.open: Why boot B's 32 KiB row is 3.93 % faster than boot A's (2.114 to 2.031 ns per load) is not explained in any file. The L1 refill drop from A to B (about 0.030 per load) is larger than the L1 prefetcher's own refills on A (0.008 to 0.009 per load). So the demand misses also dropped when the prefetcher went off. Hypothesis, not measured: prefetched lines evict chain lines at the L1 edge. No file measures this.

Regions 0 to 4 read 16.327, 16.623, 16.274, 15.295 and 14.971 GB/s [001 bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]
The CME (the Arm C1-SME2 unit on the same DSU, DSU = the Arm DynamIQ cluster) reads 36.564 GB/s from DRAM at 32 MiB in run 3 [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
The CME reads 36.899 GB/s at 2 MiB in run 3 [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]

The CRB (the Arm Neoverse V3AE reference server) reads 30 GB/s from DRAM with one core. That figure is quoted in the message to Bill and is not in any results folder [message-to-bill.md, point 5 table]

Bill raised the Asimov rate as a defect on 2026-11-04 09:26 PST: "The read throughput from DRAM is too slow. I doubt that's reality. It's probably a software mechanism issue." [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6]
why_wrong: The rate is the same at two very different latencies. The 2 MiB chase (a pointer-chase latency test, one load at a time) reads 24.096 ns per load in run 3 [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]
The 32 MiB chase reads 52.185 ns per load. So the memory itself is not the limit [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]

Little's law (lines in flight = rate x latency / line size) gives about 3.5 lines in flight at 2 MiB (9.311 GB/s x 24.096 ns / 64 B = 3.51, est.) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and latency-dram-large.csv]

It gives about 7.5 lines at 32 MiB (9.172 GB/s x 52.185 ns / 64 B = 7.48, est., or 7.56 with the flushed row's 52.738 ns) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, latency-dram-large.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv]
Bill judged 9.2 GB/s too slow to be real, against the CRB's 30 GB/s with one core [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6 and message-to-bill.md, point 5 table]
Two candidate causes were named: the core's miss-handling capacity, or the software not keeping enough loads in flight (Bill's suggestion) [message-to-bill.md, point 6]
Hypothesis H7 (the plan's name for this guess): the plain ldp loop (ldp = the Arm load-pair instruction) keeps too few lines in flight [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10, Ask 2]
A streaming read is then limited by how far the hardware prefetcher runs ahead. A software prefetch hint or a second stream should raise the rate [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10, Ask 2]

terms.definition: System level cache, the shared cache beyond the cluster's own caches. The 2 MiB buffer fits in it.
On-chip memory, a separate memory region on the chip. Run 1 read it as five regions, 0 to 4.
The Arm DynamIQ cluster. It holds the cores, their L3, and one CME.
The Arm C1-SME2 unit, one per DSU. It reads 36.6 GB/s from DRAM where one core reads 9.2 GB/s.
A mesh node that receives the memory requests for its share of the addresses. Asimov has 5 (ids 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344).
The mesh counter of requests received at one home node.
The fastest of the repeated runs of one test row.
A pointer-chase latency test. Each load waits for the previous one, so it measures one load's latency.
Lines in flight = rate x latency / line size. It turns a rate and a latency into how many 64 B lines the core holds in flight.
The number of 64 B cache lines the core has requested but not yet received.
The Arm load-pair instruction. The plain read loop uses it.
The Arm prefetch-hint instruction, asking for a line to be loaded into L1 before the loop reaches it. The tests issued it 4, 8 or 16 lines ahead.
The core's own logic that fetches the next lines of a stream without an instruction. It was off on boots B and D and on for boots C and E.
A read variant (read-2s) that reads two streams at once, meant to raise the number of lines in flight.
L1 data-cache refills caused by the hardware prefetcher, divided by lines read. A value near 1 means the prefetcher fetched nearly every line.
Core clock cycles spent per 64 B line read, at 2.003 GHz.
The plan's name for the hypothesis that the plain loop keeps too few lines in flight.
The plan's name for the group of read variants (plain, PRFM 4/8/16 ahead, two streams).
The Arm Neoverse V3AE reference server, used as a comparison point.
The home node's read-queue occupancy event. The run 7 plan proposes it to count requests in flight.
Whether the DSU's L3 cache was in full mode (boots E and F1) or off (boot C and run 3).

polished.one_line: In run 1 eight DRAM writers were no faster than four (about 88 GB/s). A firmware change then lifted both 44 to 76 %.
looked_wrong: Run 1 (membench-jibin-001, 2026-10-31): four writers, one per DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, a two-core cluster) on CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8, wrote 88.8 GB/s at 2 MiB per writer and 86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB.
Eight writers (CPUs 2 to 9) wrote 88.3 GB/s and 86.7 GB/s. Doubling the writers added nothing [001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv, best rows].
One core alone writes 32.0 GB/s at 2 MiB and at 32 MiB in run 1.

So each of four writers got 21.6 to 22.4 GB/s, and each of eight writers got 10.8 to 11.2 GB/s, far below the one-core rate [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, README 003 'Writes on the two firmware sets'].
Run 2 (membench-jibin-002, 2026-11-02) used the same write kernel and the same RTL (the hardware design source, commit 0d9e214eb43b).
Four writers wrote 127.9 GB/s at 2 MiB (+44.1 %) and 128.0 GB/s at 16 MiB (+47.5 %).
Eight writers wrote 155.4 GB/s at 2 MiB (+76.1 %) and 151.7 GB/s at 16 MiB (+74.9 %) [002 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv, best rows, README 002 lines 44 to 47].
Every other best row shared by run 1 and run 2 agreed within 3.6 % by README 002's count over 22 shared commands.
A recompute over the shared bandwidth best rows alone gives 1.80 % at most, at the pair's 48 KiB write [README 002 line 92].

The firmware had changed between the runs. SCP (System Control Processor firmware, the firmware that carries the mesh route overrides) went from 0.34.0 (release build) to 0.48.0-nopcie.1 (the box's rebuild with PCIe0 held, debug build).
TF-A (Trusted Firmware-A, the Arm boot firmware) went from 0.24.0 to 0.35.0, both debug builds [README 001 line 19, README 002 line 26, README 003 line 11].
why_wrong: In run 1, four writers and eight writers reached the same 88.8 and 88.3 GB/s at 2 MiB [001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv].
One shared limit of about 87 to 89 GB/s therefore sat somewhere in the hemisphere (the half of the Asimov chip that the emulator ran, which holds the DSUs, the home nodes and the memory behind them).
Its place (DSU, mesh port, home node, or memory controller) was unknown.
In run 2 the same multi-core write rows moved 44 to 76 %. The one-core write stayed at 32.0 GB/s.
The read and copy rows of the same commands moved under 0.5 %. A write-only change that large contradicted a stable platform [README 002 line 49].
The write kernel and the RTL were unchanged between run 1 and run 2.
The change could come from the firmware or from the code changes between the runs. The two causes were not separable from runs 1 and 2 alone [README 003 'Result'].

terms.definition: DynamIQ Shared Unit, a cluster of two C1-Nano cores that share one L2 cache. CPUs 2 and 3 sit in one DSU, CPUs 4 and 5 in the next, and so on.
The half of the Asimov chip that the emulator ran. It holds the DSUs, the five home nodes and the memory behind them. The write limit of about 87 to 89 GB/s applied to the whole hemisphere.
System Control Processor firmware, the firmware whose version carries the mesh route overrides. Run 1 used SCP 0.34.0 release, run 2 used SCP 0.48.0-nopcie.1 debug.
Trusted Firmware-A, the Arm boot firmware. Run 1 used 0.24.0, run 2 used 0.35.0, both debug builds.
The hardware design source of the emulated chip. It was the same (commit 0d9e214eb43b) in runs 1 and 2.
Run membench-jibin-003: run 2's binaries, kernel and setup rerun on run 1's firmware, to separate the effect of the firmware from the effect of the code.
The highest bandwidth of the repetitions of one command, as recorded in the result CSV. All numbers in this entry are best rows.
A mesh node that holds one slice of the SLC and forwards requests for its address range to memory. The hemisphere has five, numbered 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344.
The mesh node that sits in front of a memory controller. SCP 0.48.0 added 15 route overrides from the home nodes to the SMS nodes.
A mesh setting that forces traffic between two nodes along a chosen path (here vertical first) instead of the default path with the same hop count.
System level cache, the shared cache held in the home nodes on the mesh.
On-chip memory. OCM4's home is node 344, the node that received the extra requests on the old firmware.
Coherent Mesh Network, the Arm on-chip interconnect that joins the DSUs, home nodes and memory controllers.
The performance monitoring unit counters of the mesh, and the tool that reads them around each test row into cmn-counts.csv.
Mesh counter: requests received at one home node's POCQ. A retried request counts again.
Point-of-coherence queue, the request queue inside a home node.
Quality of service level carried by a mesh request. The cores send at QoS 14, so a cap for QoS 0 to 7 does not affect them.
The unit behind the mesh that reads and writes DRAM. Its request count (hns_mc_reqs_local_all) did not rise on the old firmware.
The per-cluster cache that was off in runs 1 to 3 and on in boot F1.

terms.definition: On-chip memory, split into five regions OCM0 to OCM4, each behind one home node on the mesh.
The mesh node that owns one OCM region and answers loads to it (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344).
One switch point of the on-chip mesh, named by its (x,y) position. Distance between two points is counted in crosspoints.
DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster that holds one pair of cores (CPUs 2-3, 4-5, 6-7, 8-9). Each DSU has one port on the mesh.
The crosspoint where a DSU joins the mesh. The question in this entry is which crosspoint holds the ports of CPUs 6-7 and 8-9.
A pointer chain the test walks to measure one load's latency. Run 2 used fresh chains, best of two passes. Run 3 used sparse chains, best of 7 passes of 64 loads per region.
A latency row whose chain spans all five OCM regions, so it reflects a CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes.
How many lines the L2 cache fetched per measured load. A value above 1 means some lines arrived before their load.
The run 4 test set of 20 cells (4 CPUs x 5 regions) that reads mesh counters at both ends of each route.
Crosspoint counters of outgoing data flits in the east, west, north and south directions. They count the data channel only.
One unit of a data message on the mesh. The read-request channel is a separate channel that these counters do not count.
A route that moves along X until it reaches the destination column, then along Y.
A fit of ns per load against the number of X steps and Y steps between a DSU port and a home node, using assumed coordinates.
Root mean square of the fit residual, in ns. A smaller value means the model matches the measured rows better.
Core hardware that fetches lines before a load asks for them. Boots B and D ran with prefetchers off, boots A and C with them on.
The RTL mesh description file that Jesse read to get the crosspoint coordinates. No local copy exists under the asimov folder.

polished.one_line: The kernel's mesh map labels home nodes by logical id. HN-S #0 to #4 are OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3, not OCM0 to OCM4.
looked_wrong: The mesh map in sysinfo.txt (the system-information dump collected on each run) prints crosspoint numbers XP #0 to #35 and each node's logical id within its type. It does not print node ids [002 sysinfo.txt:489-560].
The five HN-S cells (HN-S: a home node, the mesh unit that owns one OCM region) print #0 at crosspoint (1,3), #1 at (3,3), #2 at (5,3), #3 at (2,4), #4 at (4,4) [002 sysinfo.txt:505-536].
A node id decodes to a crosspoint as X = bits 8:6 and Y = bits 5:3. Node 88 is (1,3), 160 is (2,4), 216 is (3,3), 288 is (4,4), 344 is (5,3) [gen_hierarchy.py:51].
So HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160, 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3.
A reader who matches HN-S #n to OCMn places three of the five home nodes wrongly [002 README.md:80].
Before run 2, the node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 came only from the address map.
No perf_event_open (the Linux system call that opens a hardware counter) with bynodeid had been tried on the image [RUN2-PLAN.md:337-341, HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:33].
why_wrong: Every per-region latency claim and every mesh-distance claim depends on which home node owns each OCM region [002 README.md:31]. The expected reading was that HN-S #n in the map is OCMn.
The map looks like a node-id list but is a logical-id list. Under the HN-S #n = OCMn reading, three of the five rows (#1, #2, #3) point to the wrong OCM region.
Jesse's README states that the kernel's arm-cmn driver (the Linux driver for the mesh counters) places the HN-S filter fields one bit off this RTL's (the chip design source) [002 README.md:82].
If that offset reached the events used, per-node counts could go to the wrong node.
A wrong node id would not count the wrong node silently. The driver rejects it, and the line reads unavailable (Invalid argument) [RUN2-PLAN.md:339-341, 002 README.md:81].

terms.definition: The system-information dump run_asimov.sh collects on each run, including the kernel config, the PMU sysfs values and the mesh map.
The harness script that runs every row of a run and collects sysinfo.txt and cmn-counts.csv.
The text under /sys/kernel/debug/arm-cmn/map* that the kernel's arm-cmn driver prints: a grid of crosspoints with the nodes at each one.
A home node on the CMN mesh. Each one owns one OCM region. This SoC has five.
A requester node on the CMN mesh, the mesh port that sends requests to the home nodes.
One grid position on the CMN mesh, written (x, y). The map numbers them XP #0 to #35.
The hardware id of a mesh node. Bits 8:6 give its crosspoint X and bits 5:3 give Y. The five home nodes are 88, 160, 216, 288, 344.
A node's index within its type (HN-S #0 to #4) as the driver numbers it. It is not the node id.
One on-chip memory region, OCM0 to OCM4, each held by one home node.
The SoC's table of which address range each home node owns. Before run 2 it was the only source of the node ids.
The harness's counter reader. It opens one mesh counter per node id around a command and reports the counts in cmn-counts.csv.
The mesh counter event that counts all requests received at one home node.
The Linux system call that opens a hardware counter, with the arm-cmn option that limits the count to one node id. The driver rejects an unknown node id with Invalid argument.
The Linux kernel driver that exposes the CMN mesh counters as the arm_cmn_0 PMU.
A 4 KiB pointer-chase run on 4 KiB pages (latency --no-thp --sizes 4K --loads 8K --reps 1). It gives the background request count each node sees when no OCM region is targeted.
The streaming unit attached to each core cluster. CME rows run the same per-region tests through it instead of through a core.
The page generator that draws the mesh grid. It decodes each node id to a crosspoint and asserts the map text has an HN-S cell there.
The hardware design source of the emulated SoC. The register map and the crosspoint layout come from it.
The kernel's debug file system, mounted at /sys/kernel/debug. The mesh map is read from it.

Boot D (008, prefetchers off): 20.63 ns + 2.00 ns per X step + 0.98 ns per Y step, 0.13 ns rms. This repeats boot B. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 008 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.2]

terms.definition: On-chip memory, split into five regions (OCM0 to OCM4). Each region has a home node on the mesh.
The mesh node that serves one OCM region. A load to that region crosses the mesh to its home node.
A switch point in the mesh. The mesh distance of a cell is the crosspoint count |dx| + |dy| between the DSU's crosspoint and the home node's crosspoint.
The core cluster that holds a CPU. Each cell's distance is counted from the DSU's crosspoint.
One CPU-to-OCM-region pair in the latency test. Four CPUs by five regions give 20 cells.
A move of one crosspoint along the X or Y direction of the mesh. The step counts are assumed from mesh coordinates, not measured.
Hypothesis 5 of the follow-up run plan (follow-up-run-plan.md section 5): an X step costs more latency than a Y step.
Two layouts of the load chain in the latency test. Run 3 used the sparse chain, run 2 and the route rows the dense chain.
The lowest latency among the repeats of one cell. All the per-cell numbers in this entry are best rows.
Test labels of run 4. G2 is the dense chain of ten cells (CPUs 2 and 8) without counters. G6 is the route rows: the dense chain of all 20 cells under the mesh crosspoint counters.
The G6 rows: each cell's dense chain run with 8 crosspoint counters and a best-of-2 latency.
One unit of traffic on the mesh. The counters mxp_{e,w,n,s}_dat_txflit_valid count outgoing data flits per direction (east, west, north, south) at one crosspoint.
The mesh channel that carries the load request toward the home node (counter mxp_<dir>_req_txflit_valid). It was not counted, so the request route is unmeasured.
Root-mean-square residual of a fit: the typical miss between the fit and the measured cells, in ns.
The fraction of the variance across the cells that the fit explains. 0.75 means 75 %.
Hardware in the core (L1) and in the cluster (L2) that fetches lines before the program asks for them. On boot A's route rows the L2 prefetcher made 0.35 refills per load.
The OCM mapping of boot D: 64 KiB contiguous translations. Each unmap then adds four broadcast TLB invalidates per region.
Translation lookaside buffer, the cache of address translations. A TLB invalidate removes stale translations.
Boot E ran with the L3 cache enabled. Part of each route row's loads then hit in L3, so the fit for boot E is not usable.

polished.one_line: Sparse OCM chains read 2 to 4 ns per load above dense chains. A hashed-offset chain was faster than the sparse one.
looked_wrong: A sparse chain loads one cache line per 4 KiB page: 64 loads per pass over a 256 KiB region of OCM (on-chip memory, mapped into a process through the /dev/ocm device file).
A dense chain loads every line: 4,096 loads per pass. [latency-ocm-region0-cpu2.csv of 004, header lines=64 sparse=1]
On run 3 (result set membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03) the sparse rows read 2.31 ns per load above run 2's dense rows (membench-jibin-002), mean of 20 cells.
The range was -0.47 to +4.55 ns per load. Sparse was higher in 18 of 20 cells. [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004 and 002, README 004 lines 3 and 9]
On run 4 boot A (membench-jibin-005) the sparse rows read 3.73 to 4.33 ns per load above dense on CPU 2.
On CPU 8 they read 1.79 to 3.56 ns per load above dense. [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv and -dense-cpu<c>.csv of 005, run-4 page section 6]
On boot A the vary chain (a sparse chain with a hashed line offset per page, 64 loads per pass) was faster than the sparse chain in 10 of 10 cells on CPUs 2 and 8.
By the median of the passes it was faster by 1.72 to 6.75 ns per load (mean 3.49 ns). By best pass it was faster by 1.86 to 7.14 ns per load.

It drew prefetches at a similar rate: 1.15 to 1.73 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2, against 1.81 to 2.22 for the sparse chain. [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 005, run-4 page section 6 and table 3.4]
The dense rows' L1 TLB refills (the L1 data TLB is the core's first address-translation cache, and a refill is one miss) differed by a factor of 27 between regions on boot A.
They ranged from 0.005 to 0.136 refills per load, or 21 to 559 refills per pass of 4,096 loads. [l1d_tlb_refill_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005, run-4 page table 3.5]
why_wrong: Both chain shapes read the same region over the same path through the mesh (the on-chip interconnect). So a difference of 2 to 4 ns per load (boot A) needs a cause inside the core.
Jibin expected a much larger gap. A dense chain should hit the caches on most loads. A sparse chain should miss on every load.
So dense should have fewer refills than sparse. The gap should then be far above 2 to 4 ns per load.
This expectation is in the session transcript only, not in a result file.
Three hypotheses were written down. H2: the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset of the sparse chain.
H3: each sparse load takes one L1 TLB miss. Each load is on a new page.
H4: the 4 KiB page size is what separates the two shapes. [run-4 page section 10]
The factor-27 TLB difference between the dense regions came from mapping alignment. The kernel places each /dev/ocm mapping per process.
Each command on each boot is its own placement draw. On boot A the user-to-physical offset (va - pa) was a multiple of 64 KiB on 5 of 110 mappings.
The one dense row with a 64 KiB-aligned mapping (OCM4) refilled the L1 TLB 21 times per pass.
The four dense rows with 4 KiB-only mappings refilled 42 to 559 times per pass. [README 005 line 27, README 007 lines 58 and 124, run-4 page table 3.5]

tests.name: Vary chains (hashed line offset per page) under the prefetch counters
tests.measures: Measures prefetch refills per load (event 0x81BD) and time for the vary chain against the sparse chain on CPUs 2 and 8. A lower prefetch rate on the vary chain would support H2 (the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset). [latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv of 005]

tests.name: TLB counter set on 15 OCM rows and a DRAM stimulus
tests.run: boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Measures L1 data TLB refills (event 0x05), L2 data TLB refills (0x2D) and table walks (0x34) per load on CPU 2 for each chain shape (dense, sparse, vary) in 5 regions plus a 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages. About one L1 TLB refill per sparse load with matching walks would support H3. [latency-ocm-region<r>-{dense-,vary-,}tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005 to 010]

tests.name: Boot B: data prefetchers off through a TF-A hook
tests.measures: Measures the sparse-minus-dense gap, the vary advantage and the walk count on 4 KiB pages with the prefetchers off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1, TF-A being the Arm boot firmware). A vary advantage that disappears, or a walk count that falls to zero, shows the prefetchers caused it on boot A. [membench-jibin-006]

tests.name: Boots C and D: 64 KiB OCM translations, prefetchers on and off
tests.measures: Measures L1 TLB refills per pass and the sparse-minus-dense gap with /dev/ocm loaded with cont=1. With cont=1 each mapping sits at a user address congruent to its physical address modulo 64 KiB. Its four 64 KiB blocks carry the contiguous bit. So the TLB holds 64 KiB translations. A gap that closes would support H4. D against B shows the hint alone. C against D shows the prefetchers with the hint on both. [membench-jibin-007 commit b79dffa, 008 commit ed6056a, README 007 line 33, README 008 line 38]

tests.name: Walk rows on the sparse chains and the DRAM stimulus
tests.run: boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Measures table walks (0x34), block walks (0x8188) and page walks (0x818A) per load on the five sparse chains and the 32 MiB stimulus. A count of zero with the prefetchers off (boot D) shows the walks on the sparse chains belong to the prefetchers' requests. [latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv of 007, 008, 010]

showed: H2 not supported. On boot A the vary chain drew prefetches like the sparse chain: 1.15 to 1.73 against 1.81 to 2.22 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2.
On boot B (prefetchers off) vary minus sparse by median was -0.91 to +0.09 ns per load. Vary was faster in only 6 of 10 cells.
On boot A it was -6.75 to -1.72 ns per load, faster in 10 of 10 cells. So boot A's vary advantage came from the prefetcher.

Why the prefetcher's fills helped the vary chain more is a hypothesis without a test. [run-4 page table 3.4 and sections 6 and 11.5, timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-{vary-,}cpu<c>.csv of 005 and 006]
H3 not supported. On boot A a sparse load took 0.672 to 0.723 L1 TLB refills, 0.000 L2 TLB refills and 0.266 to 1.243 table walks (means over the timed passes).
With the prefetchers off, the walks read 0.000 per load on every sparse row on boot B, and 0.000 in all 35 passes on boot D.
With the prefetchers on, they read 0.27 to 1.24 walks per sparse load on boot A, 0.41 to 0.75 on boot C and 0.56 to 1.62 on boot E.

So the walks were translations for the prefetchers' requests, not for the chain's loads. [dtlb_walk_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005 to 010, run-4 page table 3.5 and section 13.3]
H4 supported in part. With 64 KiB translations (boots C and D) the L1 TLB refills per pass fell to 11 to 15 on every chain.
On boot A they were 21 to 559 per pass, and on boot B 25 to 599 per pass. [run-4 page table 13.1, TLB-set files of 005 to 008]
The sparse-minus-dense gap on CPU 2 (mean of the five regions, best passes) went from 4.01 ns per load (boot A) to 2.76 ns (boot C) with the prefetchers on.
With the prefetchers off it went from 1.77 ns per load (boot B) to 1.24 ns (boot D). It narrowed in 4 of 5 regions on each pair.
On boot E (L3 on, 4 KiB pages) the gap was 2.77 ns per load. The narrowing was on CPU 2 only.

CPU 8's gap widened from 2.468 ns per load (boot A) to 2.749 ns (boot C) by best pass. [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu2.csv and -dense-cpu2.csv of 005 to 008 and 010, run-4 page section 13.2, asimov-c1nano-perf.html OCM section, README 007 line 56]
Over the 69 core OCM rows, the hint alone (boot D against B) gave a geometric mean ratio of 0.985 (62 of 69 rows faster, about 1.5 %).
The hint with the prefetchers on (C against A) gave 0.977 (43 of 69 rows faster). The prefetchers with the hint on both (C against D) gave 0.861 (66 of 69 rows faster on C).
A ratio below 1 means faster on the first boot. So the prefetchers made these rows about 14 % faster, even though they widened the sparse-dense gap.
The hint changed them by about 1.5 %. [best rows of the 69 core OCM files of 005 to 008, run-4 page table 13.2]
Jesse's reading: the numbers at this spread do not decide H4. The same chain's best pass differed by up to 23.6 % between two processes of one boot (boot C), more than the mean changes.
No sparse or vary TLB-set row had a 64 KiB-aligned mapping on boot A or B.
So A against C and B against D cannot split the fall in TLB refills, or the latency change, between the contiguous bit and the 64 KiB placement. [README 007 lines 11 and 58, README 008 line 60]
polished.open: On boot D (64 KiB translations, prefetchers off) the gap is still 0.80 to 1.75 ns per load per region (mean 1.24 ns). So the page size is part of what separates the two shapes, not all of it [run-4 page section 13.2]. Still unmeasured: a boot where the sparse and vary TLB-set rows get 64 KiB-aligned mappings, to split the fall in TLB refills between the contiguous bit and the placement. Also unmeasured: why the prefetcher's fills helped the vary chain more than the sparse one.

terms.definition: On-chip memory, mapped into a process through the /dev/ocm device file.
The on-chip interconnect that carries a core's loads to OCM.
A pointer chain that loads one cache line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads per pass over a 256 KiB region.
A pointer chain that loads every cache line of the region, 4,096 loads per pass.
A sparse chain whose line offset inside each page is hashed instead of fixed, 64 loads per pass (--sparse-vary).
One traversal of the chain. The best pass is the fastest timed pass of a row. The median is the middle timed pass.
One CPU-by-region combination. Run 3 compared 20 cells (CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8 by 5 regions). Boot A compared 10 (CPUs 2 and 8 by 5 regions).
One miss in the core's first address-translation cache. The L2 data TLB (0x2D) is the second level.
A read of the page tables in memory when no TLB holds the translation. Block walks (0x8188) and page walks (0x818A) split walks by translation size.
Core hardware that fetches lines before a load asks for them. A prefetch refill is one line brought in by it.
The 15 rows of CPU 2 (5 regions by dense, sparse, vary) run under the TLB counter set, plus the 32 MiB DRAM stimulus row.
/dev/ocm loaded with cont=1: each mapping is placed so va - pa is a multiple of 64 KiB and the page-table entries carry the contiguous bit, so one TLB entry covers 64 KiB.
The offset between a mapping's user address and its physical address. The kernel chooses it per process. Each command on each boot is a separate placement draw.
Arm boot firmware. Build 0.35.0-pfoff.1 carries a hook that turns the data prefetchers off.
The level-3 cache. Boot E ran with it on.
A: 4 KiB pages, prefetchers on (membench-jibin-005). B: prefetchers off (006). C: 64 KiB translations (007). D: 64 KiB translations, prefetchers off (008). E: L3 on, 4 KiB pages (010).
The three written hypotheses: the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset (H2), each sparse load takes one L1 TLB miss (H3), the 4 KiB page size separates the two shapes (H4).
The average over rows of the ratio of best-pass times between two boots, below 1 meaning faster on the first boot named.
The row set for the boot ratios: 30 shape cells on CPUs 2 and 8, 4 all-five rows, 15 TLB-set rows and 20 route rows.

polished.one_line: With the prefetchers on, one OCM row's passes spread up to 68 % and two processes of one boot differ up to 23.6 %.

The per-region rows do not meet it. On run 3 the slow passes carry more L2 refills (correlation +0.84 within rows) and fewer L3 read refills (correlation -0.31). [004 README line 111]

tests.name: Median beside best on every OCM cell, pass time against refill counts
tests.measures: Prints the median of the passes beside the best on every OCM cell. Correlates each pass's time with the prefetch refills (event 0x81BD), the L2 refills (event 0x17) and the L3 read refills (event 0xA2). A high correlation would mean the pass time follows how many lines the prefetcher fetched. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.3 and the pass-to-pass paragraph]

tests.name: Prefetchers off as the quiet comparison, groups compared by geometric mean
tests.measures: Measures the pass spread and the process-to-process spread with the data prefetchers off. Compares groups of rows by geometric mean instead of single rows. A much smaller spread would mean the prefetchers cause most of it.

tests.name: Every CME OCM pass timed inside its own streaming span
tests.measures: Times each CME OCM pass inside its own streaming span (the ns_per_load_span column). A spread inside the span would be the prefetcher's. A spread outside it would be call cost or a wake-up.

terms.definition: On-chip memory, split into five regions OCM0 to OCM4.
The streaming unit attached to each core cluster. CME rows time loads issued through it.
A list of addresses where each load gives the address of the next load. Walking it measures one load's latency.
One complete walk of a chain. A row repeats the same chain several times and records each pass.
The fastest pass of a row. Tables quote it unless the median is printed beside it.
A chain whose lines all sit in one OCM region.
A chain of 20,480 loads over all five OCM regions with one L3 read refill per load. It is the OCM number the pages quote.

terms.term: vary chain, TLB-set row, walk row
terms.definition: Chain variants in the run 4 test set. The TLB is the core's address-translation cache.
The core's L1 and L2 hardware units that fetch lines before a load asks for them. Boots B, D and F2 ran with them off.

terms.term: L2 refill, L3 read refill, prefetch refill (0x81BD)
terms.definition: Performance-counter events. A refill is a line brought into that cache. 0x81BD counts lines the prefetcher brought in, 0x17 the L2 refills, 0xA2 the L3 read refills.
The timed streaming window of one CME pass. The ns_per_load_span column holds the time inside it, so call cost and wake-ups outside it are excluded.
A run is one result set (membench-jibin-002 is run 2, 004 is run 3). Runs 4 and 6 have several boots (A to E, F1 and F2), each a fresh start of the platform.
The difference between the best of the same chain in two benchmark commands of one boot. Each command is a new process with its own physical page placement.

terms.term: 4 KiB chase and CME round trip
terms.definition: The two control rows. The 4 KiB chase walks a 4 KiB chain from the core. The CME round trip is one call and return through the CME.

tests.name: G8 rows: L1 reads and writes, two forms, 4 to 24 KiB
tests.measures: The fixed cost per pass of each form, and the L1 rate with that cost removed. terms.definition: The level-1 cache of one core. A 16 KiB buffer sits in it.
The Arm core under test. Its core clock is 2.003 GHz, and its TRM lists an in-order pipeline.
The core's load pipes: dual 128-bit, 32 B per cycle, 64.1 GB/s at 2.003 GHz.
The core's store pipe: 128-bit, 32.0 GB/s at 2.003 GHz.
A core that cannot start later instructions before earlier ones finish. It cannot overlap a pass boundary with the next pass's loads.
A core that can run later instructions while earlier ones wait. It overlaps the pass boundary. The V3AE is one.
The Arm reference server with Neoverse V3AE cores at 2.8 GHz and a 48 B per cycle read path. Used as the core with a known answer.
The Arm Neoverse V3AE core inside the CRB.
The membench-jibin-004 run of 2026-11-03, which first showed the 58.127 GB/s row.

One repetition of the measurement. The fit uses the four best of 5 reps.
One kernel call per pass. Each pass pays the call and return cost. File bandwidth-l1-passes.csv.
All passes of a rep inside one assembly call (the --asm-passes option). File bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv.

terms.definition: System level cache: the shared cache held in the home nodes of the mesh, 3.75 MiB over five nodes once the OCM ways are locked.
On-chip memory: 4 locked ways of each home node's 1 MiB array, giving a fixed 256 KiB SRAM region per node (OCM0 to OCM4).
The mesh node that owns a slice of the address space and holds its SLC and OCM array.
One slot of a cache set. The home-node array has 16 ways, of which 4 are locked as OCM.
The cluster's streaming unit, which reads and writes memory in its own path beside the cores.
The per-cluster cache between the cluster and the mesh. It was off on run 3 and on for boot F1.
One step on the mesh. OCM3 and OCM4 sit three crosspoints from CPU 2.
A latency test that issues one dependent load after another, so each load waits for the previous one. Reported in ns per load.
A line fetched into the L3. Fewer than 1.00 refills per chase load means some lines arrived before their load.
A buffer allocated in normal memory. At 256 KiB to 2 MiB it stays in the SLC after the first pass, so warm reads are SLC-served.
The OCM method: the caches are flushed, then the buffer is streamed once. The DRAM-address rows instead use 4 to 32 warm passes.
A 2 MiB page mapping. The DRAM-address rows use it, the OCM rows use 4 KiB pages.
The device file that maps an OCM region into a process, as Normal write-back memory in 4 KiB pages.
The CMN counter event for misses in a home node's cache.
An estimate, not a measurement.

Chain load minus control is 0.372 ns on run 3 and 0.367 ns on boot E. [arithmetic on the rows above]

The Arm LLVM scheduling model lists CLASTB (the instruction that copies the last active vector element into a general register) at 12 cycles in streaming mode. [refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s line 104]

No calibration shows that the two dependency chains have the same non-memory cost. So the 0.372 ns difference is valid arithmetic but not a memory latency. [codex-review-run3.md lines 24 to 32, CME-plan.md line 473]
The page now calls it 'chain load minus round-trip baseline 0.37 ns, a derived number, not the memory latency'. [asimov-cme-perf.html, Short version]

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU, with its own 64 KiB 4-way L1 of 1,024 lines.

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit. It has its own L1 cache and its own hardware prefetcher.

A way to shuffle a list so that it forms one single cycle, used to build the random chain from a fixed seed.

terms.definition: The C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per cluster, that issues the loads in the CME rows.
A list of memory lines where each line holds the address of the next, read one load at a time.
A chain whose every line is cleaned and invalidated before each timed pass, so each load must fetch from DRAM.
A chain read for the first time during the timed pass, so no line has been seen before.
A chain small enough to be walked several times, so later passes can find its lines in a cache.
A chain whose lines come in rising address order, the easiest pattern for a prefetcher.
A unit that guesses which lines a program will need next and fetches them before a load asks.
A line brought into the CME's L1 (its first-level cache) from a level beyond it, counted per load.
A refill caused by a load that needed the line (event 0x3280).
A refill started by the hardware prefetcher before any load asked for the line (event 0x32B2).
The count of L1 refill events divided by the number of chain loads in the pass.
The main memory, reached when no cache holds the line.
The 3.75 MiB cache on the mesh.
The per-cluster cache, off on boot B and on for boots F1 and F2.
Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware that holds the hook used to turn the prefetchers off.
The timed pass length divided by the number of chain loads, the latency of one load.
The CSV row named best (core) or cme-best (CME), the fastest repetition and the value quoted on the pages.
The result folder of one run or boot: 004 is run 3, 005 boot A, 006 boot B, 010 boot E, 011 boot F1, 012 boot F2.

terms.definition: The streaming unit attached to each core cluster. It has its own L1 cache, prefetcher and TLB, and the test drives loads through it instead of through a core.
On-chip memory, held at the home nodes of the mesh. OCM0 to OCM4 are the five regions.
A switch on the mesh. Mesh distance is the number of crosspoints between the cluster and the home node, 1 or 3 here.
A pointer chain that touches one cache line per memory page.
A pointer chain that touches every cache line of the region in turn.
A third chain shape measured on boot A, slower than sparse and dense through the CME.
An L1 line fetched because a load missed in L1 (event 0x3280). At 1.000 per load, no load hit a prefetched line.
An L1 line fetched by the CME prefetcher ahead of any load (event 0x32B2).
Each row is run several times, 7 on most rows (passes cme-fresh1 to cme-fresh7). The best pass is the lowest ns per load, and the median is the middle value of the passes.
The bracket times the whole CME call. The streaming span times only the loads inside it, from in-span clock stamps.
The per-cluster cache. Boots E, F1 and F2 turned it on through a rebuilt SCP (the system control processor firmware).
The address translation cache. Boots C and D mapped OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations to test its effect.
Refills served from inside the cluster, by the L3 (event 0x327D), against refills that went out to the mesh (event 0x327E).
A reference benchmark whose OCM chase through the CME read 34.8 ns per load.

terms.definition: The cluster's SME2 streaming unit (Arm C1-SME2), one per cluster. Loads and stores can be issued through it instead of through the core.
On-chip memory. It lives in 4 locked ways of each SLC home node on the mesh, in five regions (OCM0 to OCM4), one per home node.
System level cache, held at the five home nodes of the mesh.
The mesh node that owns an address range. The own node of a region is the home node that holds that region's OCM.
The on-chip interconnect that joins the clusters to the five home nodes.
A switch on the mesh. A 3-crosspoint region (OCM3, OCM4) is three mesh steps from the core that reads it.
A cache local to one cluster. Off on boots A, B and C. On on boots E, F1 and F2.
A chain-load latency test. Each load's address comes from the previous load, so the time per load is the memory latency.
A chain on closely spaced addresses. On boot C each load pulls 2.13 to 2.66 lines from outside the cluster.
A chain on widely spaced addresses. On run 3 its loads count 0.00 to 0.03 inner refills per load.
A command that covers all five OCM regions in one chain or one read, so its requests spread over all five home nodes.
A line fill into the CME's L1 data cache from outside the cluster. Counted per load.
A line fill into the CME's L1 data cache from inside the cluster, such as the L3. Counted per load.
A line fill the hardware prefetcher started, not a demand load. Counted per load.
A line fill a demand load started. Counted per load.
The mesh counter event for requests received at a home node. Read with the cmncount tool around one command, so it covers the whole command, not only the timed loads.
The result set membench-jibin-004 of 2026-11-03. The L3 off, the prefetchers on.
Result sets of run 4 with the L3 off and the prefetchers on. They carry the dense per-region rows.

The run 4 result set with the L3 on and the prefetchers on.

Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware. The pfoff build turns the prefetchers off.
One repetition of a bandwidth command. The reported rate is the best of 3 reps.
The lifetime of one measured command in nanoseconds, as recorded in cmn-counts.csv.
