polished.one_line: On run 3 CME read calls cost about 100 ns each and write calls none. Run 6's clock stamps added about 82 ns more.
looked_wrong: Run 3 (boot 004, 2026-11-03) timed every CME bandwidth pass as one kernel call.

A line through the 16 KiB and 48 KiB read rows gives the read kernel a fixed cost of 100.6 ns per call at a slope rate of 133.5 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-read best rows 73.377 and 104.865 GB/s]
The same line through the write rows gives 0.5 ns per call at 63.9 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-write best rows 63.731 and 63.821 GB/s]
The fixed cost is 45 % of the 16 KiB read pass (100.6 of 223.3 ns).
The 1 KiB read call takes 97.1 ns on run 3. The 1 KiB write call takes 39.1 ns on run 3. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 004, best rows 10.549 and 26.213 GB/s]
The write call is 23.0 ns est. above its 16.0 ns of stores at 63.9 GB/s.
The one-load control cme-call minus the cme-roundtrip chain is only 21.7 ns per call on run 3 (42.703 minus 21.004 ns). [cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 004, rows 7 and 11]
That contradicts the 100 ns read intercept.
In run 6 the cme-call control tripled.
The best rows read 124.516 to 125.609 ns per call on boots F1 and F2 (reps up to 125.656 ns), with 61.000 to 61.250 ns of it inside the span. [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012 (24 files)]
Boot E read 42.516 to 43.609 ns per call by the best rows (reps to 43.922 ns). [cme-latency-*.csv of 010 (21 files)]
The 1 KiB read call read 186.1 ns on F1 and 191.1 ns on F2 (108.0 ns in span on both) against 97.1 ns on run 3. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read 1024 best rows]
Two run 6 forms also fit no line or no twin.
The looped write rows at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB do not lie on a line (largest residual 27.9 ns on F1 and 26.6 ns on F2). [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]
The single-call 96 KiB read reads 1.56 times its looped twin (the same size in the looped form) on F1 (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s).
On F2 it reads 1.07 times its looped twin (42.773 against 39.950 GB/s). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, 98304 best rows]
why_wrong: Every call pays the same register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP (the Arm instructions that enter and leave streaming mode) and register restore.
So a read call and a write call should carry the same fixed cost. Run 3 gave 100.6 ns for read and 0.5 ns for write, a 100 ns gap.
Hypothesis H10 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 13): stores are posted (the core does not wait for a store to finish).
The last stores of one call drain while the kernel leaves streaming mode and the next call enters. From 16 KiB up the mode switch hides behind those stores.
Hypothesis H11: the read kernel ends with a fold of its 16 accumulators (15 EOR, one EORV, one FMOV).
The fold waits for every load to return. So most of the read call's cost would be the fold and its return dependency.
Run 6's cme-call tripled for a known reason.

The run 6 kernels are run 3's plus exactly 15 instructions (2 ISB, 2 MRS of CNTVCT_EL0, 2 ADRP, 3 ADD, 1 SUB, 2 LDR, 3 STR) by Jesse's disassembly. [README 011 lines 153 and 155, and cme_kern.S header lines 11 to 23]
The ISB (an instruction barrier) before the second stamp waits for earlier instructions. So the bracket of every call now holds the stamps' own cost.
Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call, return and the second stamp's eight instructions), not the mode switch alone.

tests.name: In-span CNTVCT_EL0 stamps after SMSTART and before SMSTOP
tests.measures: Kernel time inside the streaming span (latency column 7 ns_per_load_span, bandwidth columns 11 and 12 span_s and span_GBps) against the caller's bracket around the call. Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval of one call (commit 0c190a1, five commits aa408ed to 0c190a1 on b79dffa).

tests.name: Single-call CME form, no-fold read, DSB ST write, per-call write rows
tests.measures: Each form's fitted cost per pass (four points, 2 % residual rule). Single-call at 4 to 24 KiB (cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv) and 48 to 256 KiB (cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv). Looped minus no-fold (--no-fold, cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv) as the net effect of the fold. DSB ST minus looped write (--dsb-st, cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv) as the barrier's measured effect (consistent with H10 if positive, not a proof). The per-call write size at 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB (cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv) at which the 23 ns est. disappears.

tests.name: Matched control without the stamps
tests.measures: The isolated stamp cost per call, from the same kernel with an empty span or the pre-run-6 binary on one boot. Plan section 13 G-k reading 1 says this control would be needed, and run 6 does not carry it. Section 14 for run 7 holds no such row.

showed: Single-call CME L1 read: 108.9 to 131.6 GB/s on F1 and 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on F2 at 4 to 24 KiB. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read best rows]
That is one 64-byte load per CME cycle, measured. It replaces the run 3 slope rate (133.5 GB/s, quoted earlier as 134 GB/s est.).
Single-call write: fitted rate 51.8 GB/s on F1 and 52.0 GB/s on F2 by the bracket (52.1 and 52.2 GB/s in span).
The single-call write intercept is -2.2 ns per pass. The per-size rows read 52.0 to 53.7 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]

Looped read intercept on F1: 186.2 ns per pass by the bracket, 103.9 ns in span, 134.2 ns without the fold. [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv and cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv of 011, cme-read best rows at 4096 to 24576]

On F2: 182.1, 101.1 and 138.8 ns (the F2 looped read line fails the 2 % rule, residual 6.6 ns). [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv and cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv of 012, cme-read best rows at 4096 to 24576]
So the fold costs 52.0 ns on F1 (43.3 ns on F2). Bracket minus span is 82.3 ns per call on F1 (81.0 ns on F2).
Boot E's whole cme-call without stamps took 42.5 to 43.9 ns. So most of the 82 ns is the stamps. [cme-latency-*.csv of 010, cme-call rows]
Net of the stamps a read call costs about 104 ns est. (186.1 minus 82.3 ns), near run 3's 97.1 ns 1 KiB read call.

The CME itself counted 242.7 to 246.3 cycles per cme-call on F1 and F2 against 78.8 to 87.6 cycles on run 3. So the added time runs inside the CME. [cme-latency-*.csv of 011, 012 and 004, cme_cycles_per_load column of the cme-call rows]

DSB ST (a barrier that waits for all earlier stores to finish) adds 47.4 ns per pass at 4 KiB, 97.8 ns at 8 KiB, 76.9 ns at 16 KiB and 74.3 ns at 24 KiB on F1 (48.9 to 101.5 ns on F2). [cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv minus cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]
So stores are posted. This is consistent with H10, not a proof.
Per-call writes of 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB take 124.1, 128.6, 149.8 and 182.1 ns on F1, with 76.1, 76.1, 76.3 and 90.5 ns of each outside the span. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011]
The write call's own cost stays open. The looped write gives no line to read it from. [README 012 line 176]
A call alone in its bracket spends 281.1 to 535.7 ns outside its span on F1 (280.0 to 523.6 ns on F2) in the single-call reps.
Back-to-back cme-call calls spend 63.5 to 64.6 ns outside the span. [README 011 lines 160 and 168, and README 012 line 144]
The chain rows (8,192 to 524,288 loads per span) carry 0.001 to 0.042 ns per load outside the span. The round trip reads 21.005 ns as before. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 011 and 012]

The 64-load OCM (on-chip memory at the mesh home nodes) region rows carry 4.4 to 4.8 ns per load of outside-span time over all passes (4.4 to 4.5 ns on the best passes). [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 012]
So those rows are not directly comparable with boot E's bracket values.
polished.open: Two items stay open: the stamps' own cost per call, and the write call's own cost (the looped write gives no line to read it from). A matched control without the stamps (the same kernel with an empty span, or the pre-run-6 binary on one boot) would settle the first. Run 6 does not carry it (plan section 13 G-k reading 1, no row in section 14 for run 7).

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit (codename Griffin), one per DSU cluster. The kernels drive it through Arm streaming mode.
An Arm C1-DSU cluster of two C1-Nano cores sharing one L2 cache and one CME.
The Arm instructions that enter and leave streaming mode. Every CME call pays them plus a register save and restore.
The time a call takes at zero bytes, read from a line fitted through the per-pass times at several sizes.
The bandwidth from the slope of that fitted line, in GB/s.
The caller's clock reading around the whole call, including save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call and return.
The time between two CNTVCT_EL0 stamps placed after SMSTART and before SMSTOP, inside the kernel.
The Arm virtual counter register, read with the MRS instruction to take a clock stamp.
An Arm instruction barrier. The one before the second stamp waits for earlier instructions to finish.
The read kernel's final step that combines its 16 accumulators (15 EOR exclusive-or instructions, one EORV reduction, one FMOV register move). It waits for every load to return.
Stores the core does not wait for. They drain after the instruction retires.
An Arm barrier that waits for all earlier stores to finish. Used in the --dsb-st write form before SMSTOP.
A bandwidth test that repeats the kernel call in a loop and times the whole loop.
A bandwidth test (--asm-passes --cme) that runs one call per pass and times each call alone.
The one-load latency control: one CME call that performs a single load.
The latency chain baseline whose per-load time is the CME round trip (21.0 ns).
A fitted line is accepted only when every point lies within 2 % of the line.
The fastest pass of a test's repetitions. Reps are the individual repetitions.
On-chip memory held at the mesh home nodes.
Hypotheses numbered in follow-up-run-plan.md section 13.

terms.term: run 3, boot E, boots F1 and F2
terms.definition: Run 3 is boot 004 (2026-11-03). Boot E is 010 (run 4). Boots F1 and F2 are 011 and 012 (run 6, 2026-11-06 and 07), the first boots with in-span stamps.

polished.one_line: Read streams far larger than the L3 run 2.7 times faster when the L3 is on. The counters do not show why.
looked_wrong: One core reads a 32 MiB stream at 24.546 GB/s on boot E (L3 on) and 9.196 GB/s on boot C (L3 in snoop-filter-only mode). That is 2.669 times. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010 and 007]
The two boots share one build. The L3 mode is the one change.
Boot F1 (L3 on) against run 3 (L3 off) shows the same rise on every read stream of 48 KiB and above. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
One-core reads rise 1.561 times at 48 KiB (17.483 to 27.299 GB/s) and 2.690 times at 2 MiB (9.311 to 25.044 GB/s). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
At 32 MiB they rise from 9.172 to 24.575 GB/s. One-core copies rise 1.31 to 1.75 times (17.962 to 31.438 GB/s at 32 MiB). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]

Four readers on four DSUs rise from 33.957 to 98.072 GB/s at 16 MiB (2.888 times). Eight readers rise from 66.673 to 107.593 GB/s at 16 MiB (1.614 times). [bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv of 011 and 004]
OCM reads rose too. One-core OCM reads rise 1.206 to 1.358 times (14.817 to 16.619 GB/s on run 3, 19.883 to 20.143 GB/s on F1). [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 004]
CME OCM reads rise 1.451 to 1.714 times (23.178 to 23.352 GB/s on run 3, 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s on F1). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 004]
On F1 the region's home node receives 0.46 to 0.47 times run 3's requests for regions 1 to 4 (50,227 to 50,893 against 108,075 to 109,528 per command). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004]
For region 0 it receives 0.78 times run 3's requests (84,080 against 108,176). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004]
No core write stream moved. One-core writes are 1.000 to 1.003 times (31.996 GB/s on run 3, 31.997 GB/s on F1 at 32 MiB). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
Four-DSU writes are 1.000 times (127.98 GB/s). The six writer-placement rows are 1.000 times. The all-eight write is 1.064 times at 2 MiB and 1.005 times at 16 MiB.
The CME's writes did move. Its OCM write rose from 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s (1.549 times). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011 and 004]
Its DRAM write fell from 63.865 to 42.639 GB/s at 2 MiB (0.67 times). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
No DRAM-sized chain moved. The 32 MiB random chain reads 52.185 ns per load on run 3, 52.212 ns on F1, 52.238 ns on boot C and 52.875 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-large.csv of 004, 011, 007 and 010]
why_wrong: A 32 MiB stream is 128 times the 256 KiB L3. The L3 cannot hold it. A cache that cannot hold the data was expected to leave the read rate unchanged.
The refill counters per 64-byte line are the same on both boots at 32 MiB. L1 refills are 0.9998 on boot C and 0.9998 on boot E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
L2 refills are 0.9997 on C and 0.9998 on E. L1 prefetch refills are 0.9994 on both. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
L3 read refills from the mesh are 0.0004 on C and 0.00003 to 0.00005 on E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
So each line still enters the L1 and the L2 once. The prefetcher still asks for every line.
F1's counted 2 MiB read put 0.975 times run 3's requests on the five home nodes (427,991 against 438,961 over the whole command). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, row dram-read-2M-cpu2]
It did so in 0.648 times the command time (1,391,056 ns against 2,147,182 ns). So the L3 did not take these reads off the mesh. [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, row dram-read-2M-cpu2]
One DRAM load costs 52.185 ns on run 3, 52.212 ns on F1, 52.238 ns on boot C and 52.875 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-large.csv of 004, 011, 007, 010]
At 9.196 GB/s the 32 MiB stream must overlap about 7.5 loads est. with the L3 off. At 24.546 GB/s it must overlap about 20 loads est. with the L3 on.
The core spends 13.78 to 13.93 cycles per line on boot C and 5.13 to 5.22 cycles per line on boot E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, column cycles_per_line]
The files do not record how many reads are in flight. So they do not show the mechanism.

tests.name: One-core read, boot C against boot E, with refill counters
tests.measures: It measures the one-core read rate at 2 and 32 MiB in five variants (plain, PRFM 4, 8 and 16 lines ahead, two streams). It records the refill and prefetch counters per line on two boots of one build. A rise on E with equal refills means the L3 mode, not the cache contents, changes the rate.

tests.name: Run 3's 67 core command lines rerun on boot F1
tests.measures: It measures every one-core, pair, per-DSU, all-eight and OCM read, write and copy stream with the L3 on against run 3 with the L3 off. It also counts the home-node requests of the counted 2 MiB read. A lower request count would mean the L3 serves part of the stream.

tests.name: Core page section 2.3: setup differences, speed ratios, hypotheses
tests.measures: On asimov-c1nano-perf.html (the core page) it lists which of 112 rows in 29 groups moved. It lists the nine setup items that differed between the two boots, marked high, mid or low impact. It lists three hypotheses, each with a test. A non-L3 item marked high impact would be an alternative cause.

tests.name: Proposed: reads in flight at the mesh port, prefetchers off, reader pairs
tests.measures: It would count read requests in flight at the DSU's mesh port (a CMN-S3 PMU event, to be checked in the event list) on an L3-on boot and an L3-off boot. It would rerun run 3's one-core read lines with the prefetchers off on an L3-on boot with boot F2's firmware. F2 ran only run_cme.sh. It would compare two 16 MiB readers on CPUs 2 and 3 against CPUs 2 and 4. These three tests would separate the three hypotheses listed under open.

showed: The build, the boards and run-to-run noise are ruled out. k_read, k_write and k_copy (the three stream kernels) are byte for byte the same in both builds. [run 4 boots C and E, and run 6 boot F1 against run 3]
Boot E against boot C (one build) shows the rise. [run 4 boots C and E]
The controls and the one-core writes from 48 KiB on repeat within 0.3 %. The read reps spread 1.8 % or less inside each boot. [run 4 boots C and E, and run 6 boot F1 against run 3]
Page placement is ruled out for the DRAM rows and only partly for the OCM rows.

A PRFM hint (a software prefetch instruction placed ahead of the load) lowers the rate on boot E. With the hint 4 lines ahead one core reads 20.196 GB/s against 24.945 GB/s plain at 2 MiB, and 20.353 GB/s against 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010]
On boot C the hint adds 4 % or less. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007]
With the prefetchers off and the L3 off (boots B and D) one core reads 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB. So the hardware prefetcher supplies almost all the overlap. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 006 and 008]
The sequential 8 MiB chain fell from 6.917 ns per load on boot C to 2.492 ns per load on boot E. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 007 and 010]
L1 prefetch refills per load are 0.9999 to 1.0000 on C and 0.9997 on E. That chain has its own entry. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 007 and 010]
Four readers on four DSUs read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s each on F1. That is the one-core rate. So four clusters do not share one limit. [bandwidth-perdsu.csv of 011]
Eight readers (two per cluster) read 13.4 GB/s each on F1. [bandwidth-all8.csv of 011]

The README of folder 011 (boot F1), written by Jesse, states that the home-node counts do not show the L3 taking the counted read off the mesh. It does not name a cause. [README of 011, lines 143 to 147]

The run 4 page adds a fourth reading, marked hypothesis: the prefetched lines wait in the L3 (about 11 ns from the core, est.) instead of in the SLC across the mesh. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14.3]
polished.open: Three hypotheses stand, each with a test not yet run. The L3's miss handling keeps more reads in flight per cluster. The prefetcher's requests overlap more with the L3 on. Or a per-cluster cap on reads in flight applies. A count of read requests in flight at the DSU's mesh port (a CMN-S3 PMU event) on an L3-on boot and an L3-off boot would settle which one holds.

terms.definition: The cluster's third-level cache, 256 KiB, which sits between the cores and the mesh.

terms.term: L3 on / L3 off / snoop-filter-only mode
terms.definition: Three firmware settings of the L3: full lookup and allocation (on), disabled (off), or tracking line ownership without lookup or allocation (snoop-filter-only, used on boot C).
DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds two C1-Nano cores, the L3 and the port to the mesh.
The SME2 matrix unit, one per DSU, which issues its own reads and writes to OCM and DRAM.
On-chip memory, split into five regions, each held at one home node of the mesh.
System-level cache, held at the mesh home nodes, across the mesh from the core.
The on-chip interconnect that carries requests from the clusters to the five home nodes, which hold the SLC and the OCM.
One of five mesh nodes that receives every request for the addresses it owns, and whose request counter (hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all) the record uses.
Hardware in the core that detects a stream and asks for the next lines before the program loads them.
The Arm software prefetch instruction, placed 4, 8 or 16 lines ahead of the load in the test variants.
Counter readings divided by the number of 64-byte lines read, where 1.0 means every line entered that cache once.
A latency test that follows a list of pointers, so each load waits for the previous one, which gives the cost of one load.
The number of memory reads outstanding at the same time, derived here as rate times 52.2 ns divided by 64 bytes.

A run is one execution of the command set on one firmware boot. Result folders: run 3 is 004, boot B is 006, boot C is 007, boot D is 008, boot E is 010, boot F1 is 011. Boots B and D have the prefetchers off and the L3 off, C has the L3 in snoop-filter-only mode, E and F1 have the L3 on, and F2 shares F1's firmware but ran only the CME script.
Performance monitoring unit, the hardware counters of the core or of the mesh.
An estimate derived from other measurements, not a measured value.

polished.one_line: L3 on made CME chain loads slower at 8 and 16 KiB. The L3-served load is 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load above asimov-bench.
looked_wrong: On boot E (run 4, DSU L3 on) the CME's L1 refills at 8 KiB were 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer per load, 99.5 % inside the cluster. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]
On boot C (run 4, L3 off) they were 0.59 inner and 3.33 outer per load. Means over 3 reps. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]
Yet the chain was not faster on boot E. At 8 KiB it read 24.932 ns per load against 24.466 ns per load on boot C, best rep, ratio 1.019. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
At 16 KiB it read 35.065 against 31.303 ns per load, ratio 1.120. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007 and README.md of 010 line 109]
On boot F2 (run 6, L3 on, prefetchers off) the exploratory L3-hit event 0x328E counted 0.14 to 0.64 hits per load at 96 to 384 KiB, best rep. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
Inner refills in the same rows: 0.96 to 1.00 per load, best rep (0.88 to 1.00 over all reps). [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
On boot F2 the latency fell as the chain grew: 36.0 ns per load at 96 KiB down to 32.8 ns per load at 256 KiB, best reps. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
The L3-served load on boot F2 was 32.8 to 33.9 ns per load at 192 to 384 KiB. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012]
That is 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load above the 26.6 ns per load that asimov-bench measured for the DSU L3 through the CME. [CME-plan.md line 63 and asimov-cme-perf.html open items]
why_wrong: An L3 hit inside the cluster should cost less than a refill from the mesh (the interconnect outside the cluster).
So refills moving inside the cluster should lower the chain time. Instead the chain read 1.019 times boot C at 8 KiB and 1.120 times at 16 KiB (boot E, best rep).
With the prefetchers off, every inner refill was expected to be an L3 hit. So the hit count should have been near 1.00 per load, not 0.14 to 0.64 (boot F2, best rep).
The L3-served load was expected near asimov-bench's 26.6 ns per load for the same path. It read 32.8 to 33.9 ns per load (boot F2, 192 to 384 KiB).

tests.name: Boot E against boot C: inner and outer CME refill split by footprint
tests.measures: It measures the L3's effect on the CME chain with the CME prefetcher on. It uses the inner (event 0x327D) and outer (event 0x327E) refill counters on the same commit b79dffa with only the SCP differing. A lower chain time on boot E would mean the L3 helps the CME. [README.md of 010, 'Against boot C: the L3 alone' and line 109]

tests.name: Boot F2: L3 on, prefetchers off, CME L3 events plus least-squares fit
tests.measures: It measures the L3-served chain load through the CME with no prefetch refills. It also measures which level served each refill, using the exploratory events 0x328E (L3 hit), 0x328F (L3 miss) and 0x3290 (L3 refill). A least-squares fit ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o runs over the 15 rep rows from 96 to 384 KiB. A hit count near 1.00 per load would mean the L3 served every load. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012 and README.md of 012, 'The CME L3 events' and gen_run6.py l3_fit]

showed: Boot E against boot C: the CME prefetcher's fills set the chain time on both boots. At 16 KiB boot E counted 10.4 refills per load against 7.9 on boot C (inner plus outer, means over reps). [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
The prefetch-refill event alone read 9.95 against 7.44 per load. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
So no boot E against boot C row isolates one L3 hit through the CME. The run 4 CME page lists that number as 'Insufficient data'. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]

Boot F2: the 192, 256 and 384 KiB chains read 33.910, 32.779 and 33.014 ns per load, best rep. That is 11.8 to 12.9 ns per load above the 21.005 ns per load round-trip baseline. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012, cme-best and cme-roundtrip rows]
The core's own L3 hit on boot E was 10.6 to 11.0 ns est. per load (256 and 384 KiB rows). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, 'An L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns']

Boot B (006, L3 off, prefetchers off) read 39.525, 40.700 and 41.677 ns per load for the same three chains. It counted 0.34 to 0.74 outer refills per load over the reps. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 006]

The L3 events agree with the inner/outer split by construction. Hit plus miss equals inner plus outer within 0.0001 per load, and refill equals outer, in every row. [recomputed from cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
So the events validate nothing on their own. [README.md of 012 line 182]

Hypothesis from the pre-queue check's reading of the C1-SME2 RTL: miss minus refill counts lines snooped from CPU 2's own L2, which wrote the chain with core stores while CPU 3 was offline. [evidence/jibin/prequeue-0c190a1.txt]
The least-squares fit over the 15 rep rows gives constant 23.4, L3 hit 6.7, snoop 13.9 and outer 20.4 ns est. per load, rms 0.02 ns. [README.md of 012 line 181 and gen_run6.py l3_fit]
The fit columns are near-collinear, so the split is a hypothesis, not a measurement.
polished.open: The control for the events, a chain written through the CME that no core ever touched, is not in any run. It would settle whether the hit/snoop split is real [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.2 and README.md of 012 line 211]. The 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load gap between the boot F2 L3-served load and asimov-bench's 26.6 ns per load is not attributed [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU cluster, with its own L1 cache that the chain loads go through.
The Arm DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds the cores, the CME and the cluster's L3.
Whether the DSU's L3 cache is enabled by the firmware. Boots E and F2 have it on, boots B and C have it off.
A pointer chain. Each load's address depends on the previous load, so the time per load is the memory latency.
A CME L1 refill served from inside the cluster (event 0x327D) or from outside it over the mesh (event 0x327E).
The interconnect outside the cluster that carries refills to the rest of the memory system.
The lowest ns per load value over the three repetitions of a row, the cme-best rows of a results file.
Hardware that fetches cache lines before a load asks for them. On boot F2 the prefetchers are off, so every refill is a demand refill.
A read of a line out of another core's cache inside the cluster instead of from the L3 or the mesh.
The cme-roundtrip rows of the results file, 21.005 ns per load on boot F2, the chain cost that the L3-served load is compared against.
A separate benchmark set run on the RTL. Its results came in Jacob Geldbach's package, and it gives 26.6 ns per load for the DSU L3 through the CME.
The system control processor firmware. It is the only thing that differs between boot C and boot E.
The hardware design source of the chip, here the C1-SME2 design, which the pre-queue check read to interpret the L3 events.
A line fit of ns per load against the per-load counts of L3 hits, snoops and outer refills. Near-collinear columns mean the counts move together, so the fitted costs are not firm.
Root mean square of the fit residuals, 0.02 ns here, how far the fit misses the measured rows on average.
The result folders membench-jibin-NNN for boots B, C, E and F2.

polished.one_line: A lone CME call spends 280 to 536 ns outside its timed span on boots F1 and F2, against 64 ns for back-to-back calls.
looked_wrong: Jesse's run 3 README (membench-jibin-004) bound a fixed CME (the streaming compute unit, one per core cluster) cost per timed span at 0.1 to 0.3 us est. [004 README lines 13 and 90]
That bound came from three views of the data. [004 README lines 13 and 90]

On boot E the 7 CME passes of one OCM region (on-chip memory at the mesh home nodes) spread 7.25 to 13.55 ns per load, region 2 to region 1. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-fresh1..7 rows and asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
The medians sat 3.63 to 12.66 ns per load above the bests. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-fresh1..7 rows and asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
In run 3 one cme-call rep ran 82.641 ns per call, against 43.609 and 43.625 ns in the other two reps. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv rows ocm,0,cme-call,0..2]
That is 2,498 ns over 64 calls: 5,033 extra core cycles but only 419 extra CME cycles. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv rows ocm,0,cme-call,0..2]
On boot F1, bracket minus span gave 63.5 to 64.6 ns per call for back-to-back cme-call calls (36 reps). [011 README lines 157-168 and cme-latency-*.csv of 011]
The same measure gave 76.0 to 106.2 ns per call for looped bandwidth calls of 1 to 256 KiB. [011 README lines 157-168 and looped cme-bandwidth-*.csv of 011]
Each of the 42 sparse OCM passes spent 285.8 to 292.2 ns outside its span. [011 README lines 157-168 and cme-latency-*.csv of 011]

The F1 single-call rows spent 281.1 to 535.7 ns per call outside the span: reads 281.1 to 300.9 ns and writes 354.6 to 427.8 ns after their first rep. [011 README line 168 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
Every first rep spent more, reads 348.5 to 408.0 ns and writes 476.3 to 535.7 ns. [011 README line 168 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
why_wrong: The SCP (the system control processor) sets every cluster's CME power controller to dynamic mode as each core powers on. [011 README line 349]

By the RTL (the chip's hardware description, read but not measured) a CME in dynamic mode switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us est. with both cores out of streaming mode. [004 README line 89]
Switching off cleans and invalidates its L1, and switching on invalidates the L1 again. [004 README line 89]
Every timed span follows an untimed gap outside streaming mode. Whether the CME was off at a span's start is therefore unknown. [004 README lines 13, 89 and 90]
A 64-load OCM pass would carry up to about 5 ns est. per load of such a cost, a 320-load pass 0.3 to 1 ns est. [004 README lines 13, 89 and 90]

After the bracket's two clock reads (39.0 ns, bracket_overhead_ns) and one back-to-back call are taken out, the F1 sparse passes' excess is 0.18 to 0.19 us, inside run 3's 0.3 us bound. [011 README lines 155 and 168]
The first single-call write reps' excess of 0.33 to 0.42 us is outside it. [011 README lines 155 and 168]
The files do not separate a wake-up from the rest of a call's entry and exit (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call and return). [011 README lines 155 and 168]

showed: On F1 the best pass of each OCM region spent 286.0 to 289.0 ns outside its span. All 42 sparse passes spent 285.8 to 292.2 ns. [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv and -all5.csv of 011, (ns_per_load minus ns_per_load_span) times loads]

The pass-to-pass spread of a region sits inside the span. [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011]

terms.definition: The streaming compute unit, one per core cluster, that executes the chained loads and bandwidth kernels in these rows.
The part of a CME kernel between two in-kernel clock reads (CNTVCT_EL0), covering only the loads or stores.
The outer timing around a whole call: two clock reads outside the kernel, so it includes call entry and exit as well as the span.
Bracket time minus span time, the part of a call spent on entry and exit rather than on loads.
The cost of the bracket's own two clock reads, 39.0 ns, the median of 32 empty brackets, written as comment line 3 of every CME latency CSV of 004, 011 and 012.
On-chip memory held at the mesh home nodes, read here through the CME.
One timed pass over an OCM region after a flush and a counter start, 42 such passes on a boot.
The row that times back-to-back CME calls with no loads: 36 reps on F1 and F2, 3 reps of 64 calls in run 3.
A bandwidth row in which one call stands alone in its bracket (the -asmpasses files).
A bandwidth row in which calls of 1 to 256 KiB run back to back inside one bracket.
One repetition of a row. The first rep is rep 0.
Nanoseconds per load computed from the in-span clock reads, beside ns_per_load from the bracket.
The CME power-controller mode in which the CME switches itself off after both cores leave streaming mode.
The core mode in which CME instructions execute, entered by SMSTART and left by SMSTOP.
The system control processor, which sets the CME power mode as cores power on.
The chip's hardware description. 'By the RTL' means read from that description, not measured.
The Arm virtual counter register used for the in-span clock stamps.
Hardware that fetches cache lines ahead of demand. Boot F2 ran with it off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1).
Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware. The 0.35.0-pfoff.1 build runs with the data prefetchers off.

polished.one_line: An 8 MiB in-order chain through the CME read 21.417 ns per load on boot A, the CME L1-hit time, not the DRAM time.
looked_wrong: An 8 MiB chain in address order, every line flushed from the caches first, read 21.417 ns per load through the CME on run 4 boots A, C and E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010, cme-best rows]
The CME's 4 KiB repeated chain (a CME L1 hit) read 21.453 ns per load on boot A, 21.481 ns on boot C and 21.371 ns on boot E. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]
The 8 MiB row is within 0.07 ns of the 4 KiB row on every boot. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]
The CME round-trip control (a CME call that does no memory load at all) read 21.004 to 21.005 ns per call on boots A to E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 010, cme-roundtrip-best rows]
The 8 MiB row is only 0.41 ns above the round-trip control. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 010, cme-roundtrip-best rows]
The row counted 1.00 outer refills per load (an outer refill is a line fetched from outside the cluster) on boots A, C and E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
So every line still came from outside the cluster.
The core's own walk of the same chain read 6.917 ns per load on boots A and C and 2.492 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
why_wrong: Every line of the chain is flushed before the pass. The chain is 8,388,608 bytes, 131,072 lines of 64 B. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, comment line '# size=8388608 lines=131072']
8 MiB is larger than the SLC (the system level cache, 3.75 MiB). So every line must come from DRAM once per walk.
A chain with a DRAM footprint should read at the DRAM time, not at the CME L1-hit time of 21.453 ns per load (boot A).
The measured DRAM time through the CME is 71.711 ns per load (random flushed 8 MiB chain, boot B). [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006]
The result contradicts the footprint unless something fetches each line before the load reaches it.

tests.name: CME in-order row with refill-by-cause events
tests.run: boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Counts prefetch refills (event 0x32B2, cme_l1d_refill_hwprf) against demand refills (event 0x3280, cme_l1d_refill_rd) per load, plus inner (0x327D) and outer (0x327E) refills. A prefetch count near 1.0 per load means the CME prefetcher fetched each line before its load arrived.

tests.name: Same row with the CME prefetcher off
tests.measures: Reads the row with IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 set by TF-A (the boot firmware), which turns the CME hardware prefetcher off. A rise to the DRAM time would mean the prefetcher caused the 21.4 ns.

tests.name: Row repeated on all five boots
tests.run: boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: Checks repeatability. The same value on every boot with the same prefetcher setting means the result is not measurement noise.

showed: On boots A, C and E every refill was a prefetch: 1.0000 prefetch refills per load and 2.289e-05 demand refills per load (3 demand refills in 131,072 loads). [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
The same boots counted 1.0000 outer refills per load. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
So the CME prefetcher fetched each line before its load arrived. Each load then hit the CME L1.
With the prefetcher off the row read 71.740 ns per load on boot B and 71.738 ns on boot D, with 0.0000 prefetch refills and 1.0000 demand refills per load. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]
That is 3.35 times boot A's 21.417 ns. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]
The random flushed 8 MiB chain through the CME (the DRAM time through the CME) read 71.711 ns per load on boot B and 71.712 ns on boot D. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]
The in-order row with the prefetcher off is 0.03 ns above the random flushed chain. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]
The core's chain moved the same way: 6.917 ns per load with the prefetchers on (boot A) against 52.762 ns on boot B and 52.763 ns on boot D with them off. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]
That is 7.63 times. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]
The in-order row is the stimulus a hardware prefetcher is built for.
The run-4 CME page uses it to show whether the CME prefetch event counts at all. [asimov-cme-run4.html, Words used here and section 5 chart caption]
polished.open: Open on the core side only. The core's in-order chain reads 6.917 ns per load on boot A, about one L2 hit (6.1 ns for the 128 KiB row). The core page's hypothesis is that the core's L1 prefetcher runs ahead by about one L2 hit, and the CME's runs far enough ahead for an L1 hit [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 5]. The record names no measurement that would settle this.

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine, one per DSU cluster (a DSU is the shared unit that holds a group of cores). It has its own L1 cache and its own hardware prefetcher.
A list of memory lines where each line holds the address of the next. Each load must finish before the next can start, so the time per load is the latency of one memory access.
The chain visits lines in increasing address order. This is the access pattern a hardware prefetcher is built to detect.
Every line of the chain is removed from all caches before the pass.
A load served from the CME's own first-level cache. Measured here by the 4 KiB repeated chain at 21.453 ns per load on boot A.
A CME call that does no memory load. Its time (21.004 to 21.005 ns per call on boots A to E) is the fixed cost of calling the CME.
Logic in the CME or core that notices an access pattern and fetches the next lines before a load asks for them.
A line brought into the CME L1 by the prefetcher (event 0x32B2, cme_l1d_refill_hwprf) or by a load that missed (event 0x3280, cme_l1d_refill_rd).
A line fetched from outside the cluster (event 0x327E). 1.00 per load means every line came from outside the cluster.
A CME control register bit. When TF-A (the boot firmware) sets it, the CME prefetcher is off. Boots B and D ran this way.
The system level cache, 3.75 MiB in total. An 8 MiB chain does not fit in it.
The five run-4 boots. 005, 006, 007, 008 and 010 are the result folders for boots A, B, C, D and E.
The row labelled 'best' (or 'cme-best') in a result file. It is the row the record quotes for each chain size.

polished.one_line: With the L3 on, CME writes fall from 64 to 52 and 40 GB/s. CME stores run at half a store per cycle.
looked_wrong: With the L3 on, the CME writes DRAM slower than with the L3 off.
Boot F1 (L3 on) writes 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
Run 3 (L3 off) wrote 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s at 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB. Both are bracket values, best rep. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
The drop also holds in span from 48 KiB on. On F1 the in-span write is 53.5 to 56.3 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB and 40.5 to 42.8 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. [span_GBps column of 011]
Only the 16 KiB row reads higher in span (69.5 GB/s) than run 3's bracket (63.7 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]

The core's own writes and the CME's large reads did not move. One core writes 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s in run 3 and 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s on F1. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011]
The CME reads 36.6 to 37.0 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on both. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011]
The one exception: at 160 and 256 KiB, F1's CME reads are 1.114 to 1.117 times run 3's. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011 and README 011 lines 109 and 204]
Separate from the L3 question: the CME's store rate is below its load rate on every boot.
In run 3 at 48 KiB the CME read 104.9 GB/s and wrote 63.8 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 49152-byte rows]
That is 52 and 32 bytes per cycle at 2.003 GHz. The write rate is half of one 64-byte store per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 49152-byte rows]

With the L3 on, the single-call form on F1 reads 109 to 132 GB/s, that is 54 to 66 bytes per cycle, one 64-byte load per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
The same form writes only 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s, that is 26 bytes per cycle, 0.42 of a store per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
No source on disk gives the CME store path width.
why_wrong: A cache that is turned on should not slow a streaming write that cannot fit in it. The L3 holds 256 KiB, and the write footprint is 1 to 32 MiB.
The kernels are run 3's byte for byte (checked by disassembly on the machine under test). So the change is the platform's, not the code's. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]

Run 6's in-span clock stamps do not explain the drop at 1 to 32 MiB. The outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there (118.5 to 357.8 ns of calls of 25 to 1,644 us). [README 011, bandwidth rows note]
Bracket over span is 0.995 to 1.000 at 1 to 32 MiB. [recomputed from 011 and 012]
Hypothesis on the CME page: with the L3 on, the CME's stores allocate in the L3 and drain through it at the L3's write rate. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]
The same hypothesis: with the L3 holding no data, the stores went straight to the mesh. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]
No source gives the L3's write rate as a number.
The measured CME store rate with the L3 on is 27 bytes per cycle at 48 to 256 KiB in span (53.5 to 54.8 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]
At 1 to 32 MiB it is 20 to 21 bytes per cycle (40.4 to 42.8 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]
A supporting match: one CME writing 32 MiB on F1 (40.4 GB/s) is 0.99 times the 40.9 GB/s that CPUs 2 and 3 write together (16 MiB each) on the same boot. [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011 and 004]
Run 3 also gave 40.9 GB/s for the two cores, against the CME's 62.0 GB/s then. [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011 and 004]
The page's reading (hypothesis): if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core write limit is on the cores' side, not the port's. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]

tests.name: Boot F2: CME bandwidth sweep with the data prefetchers off
tests.measures: Whether the prefetcher causes the write drop. F2 (prefetchers off by a TF-A hook) writes 51.5 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. That is 0.927 to 1.000 times F1 (2 MiB 0.927, the rest 0.992 to 1.000). So the prefetcher is not the cause [README 012 line 93 and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012].

tests.name: Single-call writes 48-256 KiB, L1 write forms 4-24 KiB
tests.measures: The store rate without per-call cost. The single-call write (--asm-passes) is 51.4 to 52.4 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB on F1 and 51.6 to 52.4 GB/s on F2. The L1 write forms (looped, single-call, looped with DSB ST) give 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB on F1. So the store rate with the L3 on is 26 to 27 bytes per cycle in every form [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011].

tests.name: Proposed: L3-event write row, L3-off write row, mixed two-core write
tests.measures: A CME write row with the exploratory L3 events 0x328E and 0x328F on, a write row on an L3-off boot with run 6's kernels, a two-core write with one core in streaming mode, and Arm's statement of the CME L1 write policy. These would show where the stores drain (L3 allocation or not). They would also show whether any of the change is the in-span clock reads. And they would show whether the 40.9 GB/s two-core write limit is on the cores' side or the cluster port's [asimov-cme-perf.html sections 6 and 10].

showed: Cause unknown. The CME page lists it as open ('open: why the CME's writes fall with the L3 on'). [asimov-cme-perf.html section 10]
Two causes are ruled out. F2 rules out the prefetcher: its writes are 0.927 to 1.000 times F1's at 16 KiB to 32 MiB. [README 012 line 93]
The stamp check rules out run 6's clock reads at 1 to 32 MiB: the outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there. [README 011, bandwidth rows note]
The CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters. The bandwidth program refuses --perf together with --cme. So no refill count sits beside the drop. [README 012 line 142]

Side result from F2: the CME prefetcher carries about half of a streaming DRAM read. The CME read at 32 MiB is 17.7 GB/s on F2 against 36.6 GB/s on F1 (0.48 times). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012 and 011]
Copies fell with the writes. CME DRAM writes and copies on F1 are 0.65 to 0.84 times run 3's by the bracket at every size, and 0.65 to 0.89 times in span from 48 KiB on. [README 011 line 11]

Page defect found during verification: the 'CME L1 on its own' row of asimov-cme-perf.html prints an unrendered template, '{BPC6 * max(SINGLE_WR) / 64:.1f} of a store per cycle', where the number 0.42 should appear. [asimov-cme-perf.html table 'The CME L1 on its own']
The generator should be fixed.
polished.open: Where the CME's stores drain with the L3 on is still unknown. The 40.9 GB/s two-core write limit is not yet assigned to the cores or to the cluster port. A CME write row with the exploratory L3 events 0x328E and 0x328F on, and a write row on an L3-off boot with run 6's kernels, would settle whether the stores allocate in the L3.

terms.definition: The cluster's Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU cluster, that runs the streaming load and store kernels.
Arm DynamIQ Shared Unit: one cluster of cores with one CME and one L3. CPUs 2 and 3 are in the same cluster as the CME measured here.
The cluster's 256 KiB cache. Run 3 had it off, run 6 had it on.
The on-chip interconnect that joins the clusters to the memory system.
The 2026-11-03 UTC run (membench-jibin-004) with the L3 off.
The run of 2026-11-06/07 UTC whose boots are F1 (membench-jibin-011) and F2 (membench-jibin-012).
Run 6 boot of 2026-11-06 UTC (membench-jibin-011) with the L3 on and the prefetchers on.
Run 6 boot of 2026-11-06/07 UTC (membench-jibin-012) with the L3 on and the data prefetchers off.
Short forms of the result directories membench-jibin-004 (run 3), membench-jibin-011 (boot F1) and membench-jibin-012 (boot F2). 'README 011' is the README in membench-jibin-011.
asimov-cme-perf.html, the report page for the CME tests.
The timer around the whole call, so it includes per-call cost.
The clock stamps inside the streaming span, so the outside-span interval is excluded (span_GBps column).
The part of a call that lies outside the clock stamps: 118.5 to 357.8 ns of calls of 25 to 1,644 us at 1 to 32 MiB on F1.
The fastest repetition of a bandwidth measurement. The quoted bracket numbers use it.
Every pass of a rep inside one call (the --asm-passes rows), which removes per-call cost.
One of the L1 write forms. 'Looped with DSB ST' is the same form with an Arm store barrier (DSB ST) added.
Bandwidth divided by the 2.003 GHz core clock. A 64-byte line per cycle is one load or one store per cycle.
How many bytes the CME can store per cycle. No source on disk gives it.
The hardware unit that fetches data ahead of demand. Turned off on F2 by a TF-A hook that sets IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28.
Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware that runs before the operating system and can set core control registers.
The Arm SME mode in which a core's loads and stores go through the CME.
Performance counter events for the L3 that the proposed write row would turn on to see whether stores allocate in the L3.
Two options of the bandwidth program. It refuses them together, so CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters.
The path from one DSU cluster to the mesh. The hypothesis asks whether CME stores and core stores share it.
Two cores in the same cluster as the CME. Their two-core write of 16 MiB each gives 40.9 GB/s on both run 3 and F1.

polished.one_line: On boot E an 8 MiB chain of flushed DRAM lines reads 2.492 ns per load, under the L2 hit's 6.023 ns.
looked_wrong: The sequential chain is an 8 MiB chain (a list of loads where each load returns the address of the next) over the 64-byte lines in address order.
Every line is flushed from every cache before each pass. So every load of it is a DRAM read [core page glossary, latency-dram-seq.csv header flush=1 seq=1].
On boots A and C (run 4, prefetchers on, L3 off) the chain reads 6.917 ns per load, best of two fresh passes [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 007].
On boot E (run 4, prefetchers on, L3 on) it reads 2.492 ns per load (fresh1 2.501 ns, fresh2 2.492 ns) [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010].
The prefetch counters are the same on all three boots: 1.0000 L1 refills and 1.0000 L2 refills per load [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010, 005, 007].
The L1 refills requested by the hardware prefetcher read 0.9997 per load on E, 0.9999 on A, and 1.0000 and 0.9999 on C [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010, 005, 007].
On boot E the 4 KiB repeated chain (an L1 hit) reads 2.002 ns per load (4.01 cycles).
The 128 KiB repeated chain (an L2 hit) reads 6.023 ns per load on E and 6.096 ns on A [latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 005].
So on boot A the DRAM stream costs about an L2 hit. On boot E it costs 4.99 cycles at 2.003 GHz, one cycle above the L1 hit.
The L3 read refill event 0xA2 reads 0.0001 per load on boot E's sequential chain. Yet every line was flushed and came from outside the DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds the L3).
On the random flushed chain of the same boot it reads 1.0001 per load [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010].
why_wrong: Every load is a DRAM read: the line is flushed first, and one L2 refill per load is counted.
Yet one load costs an L2 hit on boots A and C (6.917 ns against the 6.096 ns L2 hit on A).
On boot E one load costs an L1 hit plus one cycle (2.492 ns against the 2.002 ns L1 hit) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 010].
One DRAM read costs 52.659 ns on boot E's random flushed chain [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010]. A 2.492 ns load cannot be waiting for its own line.
The L3 is 256 KiB per cluster. It cannot hold an 8 MiB stream.
So the 2.78 times change from boot A to boot E (6.917 / 2.492) with the same prefetch counts per load has no cause in the counters on disk.
Jesse's boot E README says the same: "These files do not show why its latency fell" [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md line 113].
The excess over the L1 chain on boot E is 0.490 ns (2.492 minus 2.002). That is 0.98 cycles at 2.003 GHz, close to one whole cycle.
A wait for a late line would not average to a whole cycle [core page section 8].

tests.name: Sequential 8 MiB chain (--seq), prefetch event set, core and CME
tests.run: boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E
tests.measures: It measures ns per load and demand against prefetch refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 (events 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2, 0x81BC, 0x81BD, 0x0111) on results 005 to 010. The same row runs through the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine, one per cluster, file cme-latency-dram-seq.csv). It also checks that the prefetch events count at all. The sequential chain is the prefetch stimulus [follow-up-run-plan.md line 16].

tests.name: Sequential row with prefetchers off and L3 on (boot F2 firmware)
tests.measures: It would show how much of the 2.492 ns per load on boot E is the prefetcher's. Neither run 6 boot measured that. F2 (results 012) ran run_cme.sh only. F1 (results 011) ran run_all.sh at commit 0c190a1 with no latency-dram-seq.csv [run 4 core page section 14.2, README of 012 line 3].

tests.name: Sequential chain with two members per line (32-byte stride)
tests.measures: A per-line cost would halve per load, and a per-load cost would not [core page section 8].

tests.name: Sequential-chain row under the L1 hit counters
tests.measures: It would show whether any load waited for a line that had not yet arrived. The refill counters cannot say that [core page section 8].

showed: The DRAM time is overlapped, not missing.
With the prefetchers off (boots B and D, L3 off) the same chain costs the full DRAM time, 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load.
That matches the random flushed chain (52.659 ns on boot E, 52.739 ns on boot B) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008, 010].
So address order alone gives no gain. The prefetcher does the overlap.
On boot E the prefetcher issues a new DRAM read every 2.492 ns. Each read takes about 52.7 ns.
So it keeps about 21.2 reads in flight (issued and not yet returned) (est., 52.762 / 2.492).
On boot A it keeps about 7.6 reads in flight (est., 52.762 / 6.917) [derived from latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 005, 010, core page section 8].
The stream rate on boot E is 64 bytes per 2.492 ns, 25.7 GB/s (derived, GB = 1e9 bytes).
That is about the plain one-core DRAM read of the same boot: 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010, best rows].
On boot C the plain read moves 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007].
By the same arithmetic boot C keeps about 2.8 times fewer reads in flight (est.).
The CME's own sequential row is unchanged by the L3: 21.417 ns per load on boots A, C and E alike, with 1.0000 prefetch refills per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010].
Four hypotheses are on the pages, none tested.
(1) With the L3 holding data, the prefetcher's stream drains into the L3 and the L2 refills complete sooner [run 4 core page 14.2].
(2) The full-L3 mode lets the cluster keep more read requests in flight toward the mesh [core page 2.3].
(3) The extra whole cycle per load is the prefetched line's write into L1 taking the cache for one cycle per line [core page section 8].
(4) Either the L1 prefetcher's fills do not allocate in the L3, or event 0xA2 counts demand reads only. The TRM (the Arm Technical Reference Manual) text does not say which [run 4 core page 3.1].
polished.open: What the L3 changes in how far ahead the prefetcher runs is unknown (Insufficient data) [core page section 8]. The sequential row with the prefetchers off and the L3 on (boot F2's firmware) would show how much of the 2.492 ns per load is the prefetcher's. A 32-byte-stride chain would show whether the cost is per line or per load.

chart.takeaway: Every load of the sequential chain is a DRAM read, yet on boot E it costs 2.492 ns, one cycle above the L1 hit and under the L2 hit. With the prefetchers off the same chain costs the full 52.762 ns DRAM read.

terms.definition: An 8 MiB chain of loads whose members are the 64-byte lines in address order, with every line flushed from every cache before each pass, so every load is a DRAM read.
A list of loads where each load returns the address of the next load, so the loads cannot overlap on their own.
A chain that fits in one cache level and is read again and again, so each load is a hit in that level (4 KiB for L1, 128 KiB for L2).
An 8 MiB chain in random address order with every line flushed before each pass, which gives the cost of one DRAM read with no prefetch help (52.659 ns on boot E).
Hardware in the core that notices an address pattern and fetches the next lines before the program asks for them.

terms.term: L1 refills requested by the hardware prefetcher
terms.definition: The per-load count of L1 cache fills that the prefetcher asked for rather than the program (events 0x81BC and 0x81BD).
The counter of L3 accesses that receive data from outside the L3 due to a memory read, per the TRM text.
DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds the shared L3 cache.
The Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine, one per cluster, which runs its own loads beside the cores.
The five run 4 boots (results 005, 006, 007, 008 and 010): A and C have prefetchers on and L3 off, B and D have prefetchers off and L3 off, E has prefetchers on and L3 on.
The two run 6 boots (results 011 and 012) with the L3 on. F2 ran only the CME tests.
One timed pass over the chain after all its lines were flushed, so the pass starts with nothing cached.
The ns per load times the 2.003 GHz core clock, as written in the CSV column cycles_per_load.
DRAM reads that have been issued and have not yet returned their data.
The Arm Technical Reference Manual for the core, which defines what each performance event counts.

polished.one_line: Boot E's sparse OCM rows read faster than on the L3-off boots, with fewer outside refills per load. The L3 serves part of their loads.
looked_wrong: Boot E (run 4, membench-jibin-010, 2026-11-05) is the first boot with the L3 in full mode for CPUs 2 to 9.
Its sparse per-region OCM rows from CPU 2 read 19.078 to 20.391 ns per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv of 010, best row]
On run 3 (L3 off) the same rows read 21.359 to 25.781 ns per load, and on boot A (L3 off) 22.859 to 27.594 ns per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv of 004 and 005, best row]
Against boot A, the 10 sparse cells of CPUs 2 and 8 on E read 0.69 to 1.10 times A's time.

The one cell above A was CPU 8 to OCM4. It read 23.906 ns per load on E, against 20.141 ns on run 3 (+18.7 %) and 21.813 ns on A (+9.6 %). [latency-ocm-region4-cpu8.csv of 010, 004 and 005, best row, and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14]
The dense all-five control row did not move.
From CPU 2 it read 26.082 ns per load on E, against 26.009 ns on A, 24.959 ns on C and 25.340 ns on run 3. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 010, 005, 007 and 004, best row]

The sparse rows counted fewer L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load on E. They counted 0.33 to 1.00 over the 10 cells of CPUs 2 and 8, 9 of them below 0.8. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
CPU 2 alone counted 0.330 to 0.589 per load on E, 0.739 to 0.772 on A and 0.703 to 0.830 on C. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, 005 and 007, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
The anomaly is this drop in outside refills together with the drop in time.
Two more signs on E.
Jesse's boot E README counts up to 0.48 L2 refills per load on the OCM passes that neither prefetch event nor 0xA2 accounts for, against at most 0.0157 on A. [membench-jibin-010/README.md line 153]
The route rows read 13.972 to 23.190 ns per load with 0.415 to 0.824 outside refills per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-route-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 010, best row]
why_wrong: Every OCM load should cross the mesh to the region's home node. So each load should count one outside refill, that is 1.0 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load.
The L3 is 256 KiB per two-core cluster. One OCM region is also 256 KiB.

The /dev/ocm module maps a region as Normal write-back memory, the cacheable memory type. So the L3 may hold OCM lines. [membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 34 and 37, membench-jibin-010/README.md lines 318 and 319]
A sparse chain touches 64 lines per pass. Lines from the pass before can still be in the L3 when the next pass runs.

An L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns est. (from boot E's hit set, 10.6 ns at 256 KiB and 11.0 ns at 384 KiB). A mesh round trip costs about 26 ns. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 5, derived from latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 010 and 007]
So a row with part L3 hits reads below the true OCM latency.

tests.name: Dense all-five control row kept on every boot with the 0xA2 counter
tests.measures: Whether every load still comes from outside the cluster when the L3 is on. A count of 0xA2 per load at 1.0 means no L3 hits. This row is then the OCM number to quote. On F1 it ran from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8.

tests.name: Run 3's 20 sparse rows repeated byte for byte on L3-on firmware
tests.measures: The share of sparse-row loads served from the mesh (0xA2 per load) against run 3. The L2 refills per load serve as the control that the chains miss the L2 the same way. It ran from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8.

tests.name: Proposed: sparse rows run under the L3 hit event (0x81C6)
tests.measures: Which loads hit the L3, as a direct count instead of the difference in 0xA2 counts. 0x81C6 is the hit event of boot E's hit-set event group.

tests.name: Proposed: hit-set row from CPUs 4, 6 and 8, L3 on
tests.measures: Whether the L3 of the other clusters is in full mode too. Boot E's register read and hit counter cover CPU 2's cluster only.

showed: On E the dense all-five chain from CPU 2 counts 1.0010 and 1.0005 outside refills per load in its two passes (mean 1.0008). CPU 8 counts 1.0009 per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, fresh1 and fresh2 rows, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
So none of the dense chain's loads is an L3 hit. This row is the OCM number to quote.

Boot F1 (run 6, membench-jibin-011, 2026-11-06) repeats the dense all-five row from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 at 25.536, 25.932, 25.445 and 27.702 ns per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, best row]
It counts 1.0007 to 1.0009 outside refills per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, best row]

polished.one_line: On boot D, two processes running the same 32 MiB chain counted 0.0034 and 0.4376 table walks per load, a 129 times gap.
looked_wrong: Boot D ran one 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages in two processes.

The first process (the TLB-set row) counted 0.0033 and 0.0035 walks per load (event 0x34, DTLB_WALK), mean 0.0034. Its best pass ran at 53.266 ns per load. [008 bootD latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best, column dtlb_walk_per_load]
The second process (the walk row) counted 0.4381 and 0.4371 walks per load, mean 0.4376. Its best pass ran at 58.725 ns per load. [008 bootD latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best]
That is 128.7 times more by pass means. By the best passes it is 132.8 times more (0.4381 against 0.0033). [008 bootD latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best]
Boots C and E showed smaller gaps.

Boot C's gap went the other way: 0.3669 and 0.3655 walks per load in the TLB-set row against 0.1849 and 0.1850 in the walk row. [007 bootC latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
Boot E read 0.3662 and 0.3655 against 0.5113 and 0.5118. [010 bootE latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]

Event 0x8188 (DTLB_WALK_BLOCK) read 0.0000 in all 37 pass rows of each boot's six walk files on boots C, D and E. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
Event 0x818A (DTLB_WALK_PAGE) equalled 0x34 to four decimals on every 32 MiB pass. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
On the five sparse OCM walk rows of boots C and E (prefetchers on), 0x34 counted up to 2.6094 and 2.7969 walks per load. [007, 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]

On those rows 0x8188 read 0.0000 in all 70 passes. 0x818A read 0.0156 (one walk in 64 loads) in two boot C passes only. [007, 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4, the two 0.0156 readings in 007 region1 row fresh5 and region2 row fresh7]
On boot D (prefetchers off) all three events read 0.0000 in all 35 OCM passes. [008 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
why_wrong: A walk rate on one chain was expected to belong to the boot (its page size and firmware), not to the process.
Boot D's 0.003 walks per load looked like the effect of the contiguous hint (boot D mapped the OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations).
But the hint changes only the /dev/ocm mappings. The 32 MiB chain lives on 4 KiB DRAM pages.

The rate was already spread across boots before the hint. Boot B read 0.3657 and 0.3661 walks per load on this row (58.509 ns best). Boot A read 0.5204 and 0.5210 (58.810 ns best). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13, 008 README section Against boot B, and 005 and 006 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv]
A counter that never reads nonzero (0x8188) cannot be told from one that does not count.

By the RTL (the chip's hardware source code), 0x34 counts a data-side walk when it starts. Walks for the prefetch requesters (ids TLBID_PF0 to TLBID_PF3) are included. [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359 and :1368, nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376 and :3405-3414, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]

0x8188 and 0x818A count a walk only when it returns a fault-free translation to the core. [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359 and :1368, nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376 and :3405-3414, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]
On this RTL a walk that ends in a page entry with the contiguous bit counts in 0x8188, not 0x818A. [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3147]
A nonzero 0x8188 on a boot C or D OCM row would have shown the walker using the hint. It read 0 there. [007 and 008 READMEs, The walk rows]
But the OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counted returned no translation to the core. So those zeros do not test 0x8188. [007 and 008 READMEs, The walk rows]

polished.open: Why two processes of one boot differ is Insufficient data. The DRAM chain's physical pages are not logged (the dmesg map lines cover /dev/ocm mappings only). No file shows what started each walk or how it ended [007 README, OCM mappings]. Running the same chain in several walk-counted processes of one boot would show whether the rate follows the process's page placement. Adding 0x813C (DTLB_WALK_RW, a demand-only walk event that no run's counter set included) would separate the program's walks from the prefetchers' walks [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, open items, and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 7].

terms.definition: A random pointer chain: each load's address comes from the value the previous load returned, so the loads cannot overlap.

terms.definition: One start of the test system on which a set of test rows ran. Run 4 had boots C and E (result folders membench-jibin-007 and 010). Run 6 had boots F1 and F2 (folders 011 and 012).
The sixteen one-core L1 bandwidth rows: read and write at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB, each in a looped form and a single-call form.

Two ways to run the same L1 row. The looped form repeats passes over the buffer in a loop (file bandwidth-l1-passes.csv). The single-call form does the work in one call (file bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv).
The first-level data cache of one core, 32 KiB. A 4 KiB buffer fits in it.

Core clock cycles spent per 64-byte cache line read. Lower is faster.
Lines fetched into the L1 from a lower level, per line accessed. A value near zero means the buffer stayed in the L1.

The rows that fit the 32 KiB L1 (first-level cache) did not repeat.

The one-core 16 KiB read gave 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 58.127 GB/s on run 3 (0.965 times). The three reps were 55.715 to 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 57.654 to 58.127 GB/s on run 3. [004 and 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
The pair 16 KiB read gave 112.409 GB/s on F1 against 116.407 GB/s on run 3 (0.966 times). [004 and 011 bandwidth-pair.csv]

The one-core 16 KiB write gave 30.608 GB/s on F1 against 30.127 GB/s on run 3 (1.016 times). The F1 write value is back at the 30.578 to 30.579 GB/s of runs 1 and 2. [001, 002, 004, 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
The one-core writes of 48 KiB to 32 MiB repeated within 0.3 % (F1 over run 3: 1.000 to 1.003). [004 and 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
The pair writes at 48 KiB and 160 KiB did not repeat (1.049 and 1.233). [004 and 011 bandwidth-pair.csv]
The mesh counters (cmn-counts.csv, column child_elapsed_ns, which spans the whole command) showed that F1's core latency commands ran longer.
The four counted 4 KiB controls took 1.310 to 1.423 times run 3's command time. The 20 single-region sparse OCM (on-chip memory) rows took 1.236 to 1.598 times.
The four sparse all-five rows took 1.167 to 1.208 times. The dense all-five rows took 1.028 to 1.044 times.
The three 2 MiB SLC (system level cache) chains took 1.010 to 1.024 times. The uncounted 4 KiB control took 1,269,307 ns on F1 against 883,269 ns on run 3 (1.437 times). [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv]

The timed passes inside those commands did not grow. The four counted controls read 2.015 to 2.020 ns per load on F1 against 2.012 to 2.019 ns per load on run 3. [004 and 011 latency-control-cpu*.csv]

The 20 sparse OCM rows got faster: best 17.266 to 22.609 ns per load on F1 against 20.141 to 28.453 ns per load on run 3 (0.693 to 0.953 times, all 20 cells below 1). [004 and 011 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv]

The counted core bandwidth commands ran 0.648 to 1.027 times run 3's command time. The counted 2 MiB read took 1,391,056 ns on F1 against 2,147,182 ns on run 3 (0.648 times). [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv]
why_wrong: A 16 KiB buffer fits the 32 KiB L1. The L3 (the third-level cache, the platform change that F1 was run for) should not touch it.
The kernels k_read, k_write and k_copy (the bandwidth inner loops) are byte for byte the same in both builds.
So an L1-sized row should repeat. It did not.
For the latency commands, the timed passes repeated or got faster. The whole command ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer.
So something outside the timed passes grew.
The mesh counters give one time per whole command (chain build, flushes and unmap included). They cannot say which part grew.
Nine setup items differed between the two boots.
The SCP (system control processor) firmware was 0.48.0-nopcie.1 on run 3 with L3 full mode for cluster 0 only, and 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 on F1 with L3 full mode for clusters 1 to 4 too.
The /dev/ocm module build differed (F1's adds debug map lines and the clusterpwrstat file, with the same 4 KiB mapping).
The binaries differed (commit ba834c0 on run 3 against 0c190a1 on F1): pass and worker differ, with the --asm-passes, --perf and CME paths.
chase (the latency program's loop) is the same 34 instructions. Its 48 B loop sits inside one 64 B line on F1 and across two lines on run 3.
k_write sits 16 B later in its line. [011 README lines 80-88, perf page section 2.3]
The latency rows on F1 carried three more prefetch counter columns (no multiplexing, perf_cov 1.0000).
The init differed: F1 ran the box's wrapper, which ran cme_test for about 0.012 s before run_all.sh.
Both boots ran on CPU 2 under SCHED_FIFO 10 (a real-time scheduling class and priority) with RT throttling off. So the scheduling is the same.
The emulator boards differed (ga13pd02 boards 6 to 9 on run 3 against 18 to 21 on F1, the same image copy). The dates differed. [011 README lines 80-88 and 322, perf page section 2.3]

A per-part timer (chain build, flushes, unmap, timed passes) on both builds would settle the second.
