polished.one_line: On the CRB, repeated random chains read 5.4 to 6.8 ns despite missing L2. Writers split across two meshes lost over half their bandwidth.
looked_wrong: Learned chain. On the CRB (the Arm Phoenix reference server board: Neoverse V3AE cores, two CMN meshes, CMN being the Arm coherent mesh network) a random chain (a list of pointers walked one load at a time) walked a second time read 6.784, 5.626 and 5.424 ns per load at 8, 16 and 32 MiB in the main sweep of 2026-10-30. [crb/results/20261030T193108Z/latency.csv best rows]
The counters showed every load missing the 2 MiB L2 (the per-core second-level cache).
One pass over a chain never walked before read 26.093 ns per load at 8 MiB and 30.668 ns at 56 MiB. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv best rows]
Cross-chiplet chain. A chain built on one chiplet (one of the two CRB dies, each with its own mesh) and walked from the other was first quoted as 2 to 7 ns extra per load.
That quote took the best of two 32 MiB walks: 32.72 to 37.29 ns per load against 30.22 to 30.25 ns on the same chiplet.

At 16 MiB the first walk cost 84.95 to 88.46 ns per load, the second 31.74 to 33.23 ns, and a same-chiplet walk 29.03 to 29.12 ns. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv, fresh1, fresh2 and best rows]

Write collapse by thread count. In the CRB follow-up of 2026-10-30, DRAM write bandwidth fell as threads were added: 393.96 GB/s with 64 threads, 149.45 GB/s with 96 threads and 141.18 GB/s with 120 threads. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv rows 259, 274, 289]
One writer at 8 MiB reached only 73.15 GB/s. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv row 102]

Write collapse by placement. The placement grid of 2026-11-02 gave 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh, 172.81 GB/s with 32 writers on each mesh and 346.49 GB/s with 16 writers on each mesh. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv best rows]
Readers split 32+32 still gave 327.91 GB/s, against 346.05 GB/s with 64 readers on one mesh. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/readgrid.csv best rows]
SLC capacity. The cache that sysfs (the Linux kernel's hardware description files) lists as L3 is the 128 MiB SLC (system level cache, held in the mesh home nodes).

In the CRB uncore run of 2026-10-30 (the run that read the mesh counters) a single buffer missed in the SLC 0.11 times per load at 64 MiB, 0.81 times per load at 96 MiB and 1.17 times per load at 128 MiB. [crb/results/uncore-20261030T203537Z/cmn-{64M,96M,128M}-{long,short}.csv, long minus short, over chase-long.csv minus chase-short.csv loads]
96 MiB is well below the 128 MiB size.
why_wrong: A load that misses L2 cannot complete in 5 to 7 ns on this board. The never-walked chain shows the true miss cost: 26 to 31 ns per load at the same sizes.
The V3AE core has a temporal prefetcher (hardware that learns a repeated miss sequence and refills L2 before the next load arrives).
homelat.c (the CRB core-to-slice latency program) saw the same effect. With one fixed order its timed passes fell from 30 ns to 7 ns from the second repeat on. [bench/homelat.c:646-648]
Reporting the best of N walks hides the cost of the first touch (the first walk over lines held on the other chiplet).
At 16 MiB the two cross-chiplet walks differ by 53 to 56 ns per load. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv]
Adding writers should not lower the total.

The CRB page (crb-memory-hierarchy.html) reads the fall as a placement effect: the collapse starts once both meshes carry about 32 writers or more. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'Writers on both meshes collapse DRAM write bandwidth']
The 64 MiB knee is the per-mesh SLC capacity.
Each mesh has 64 HN-S home nodes (mesh nodes that each own one slice of the SLC) of 1 MiB each (est.). [crb/results/cmn-map.txt, 64 numbered HN-S nodes per map]
A buffer is interleaved line by line, half on each mesh. [crb-hierarchy-findings.md, root run 2026-11-02]

tests.name: latency.c --fresh K and --flush: one pass over an unseen chain
tests.measures: Times one pass over a chain the core has never walked. --fresh K in bench/latency.c builds K = 2 to 8 chains per line. --flush in asimov/latency.c runs DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction) on every line before the pass. A result near 26 to 31 ns per load means a true miss. A result far below it means a prefetcher learned the chain [bench/latency.c:166-183, 222 and asimov/latency.c:17-18, 348 and run 1 CSV headers 'fresh=3 flush=0' in latency-dram-large.csv and 'fresh=0 flush=1' in latency-dram-flushed.csv].

tests.name: latency.c --build-cpu with a per-walk report instead of best-of-N
tests.measures: Builds and first-touches the chain on one core and walks it from another, reporting each walk on its own. A large gap between the first and the second walk means a first-touch cost that best-of-N hid [bench/latency.c:140-161 and crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv].

tests.name: Writer and reader placement grid, 16 to 64 per mesh
tests.measures: Measures DRAM write and read totals by how many threads sit on each mesh. A total that depends on placement rather than on thread count means a mesh-level effect [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv, readgrid.csv].

tests.name: homelat.c core-to-slice latency with a new random order per repeat
tests.measures: Measures latency from one core to the nearest and the farthest SLC slice with a new random order for the fill and the evictor on every repeat. The prefetcher then cannot learn the order. The result is the true slice latency [bench/homelat.c:51, 628-669 and crb/results/sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv].

tests.name: Part 5 write-path counters on one writer
tests.measures: Counts L1 and L2 refills-for-write, write-backs and crosspoint credit stalls while one writer runs. Zero stalls outside the core mean the single-writer limit sits inside the core [crb/results/sudo-20261102T211150Z/writepath.csv].

tests.name: Asimov fresh random chains, L2 prefetch-refill counter, prefetchers on and off
tests.measures: Counts L2 refills caused by a hardware prefetcher (PMU event 0x81BD, PMU being the performance monitoring unit) per load on fresh random chains with the prefetchers on (boot A). Re-times the same rows with them off (boot B). Zero refills with no timing change mean the C1-Nano (the Asimov core) does not learn a random chain [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.2 and section 11.2].

showed: Never-walked chains on the CRB read 26.093 to 30.668 ns per load from 8 to 56 MiB. So the 5.4 to 6.8 ns learned-chain values were prefetcher hits, not misses. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv]
The cross-chiplet first walk cost 84.95 to 88.46 ns per load at 16 MiB. That is about 56 to 59 ns more than a same-chiplet walk. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv]
The CRB page replaced its 2 to 7 ns claim with 'A first read of lines cached on the other chiplet costs 85 ns, later reads 32 ns'. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html]

The write collapse is a placement effect across the two meshes: 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh against 172.81 GB/s with 32 writers on each. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv]

The root run of 2026-11-02 (run with root rights, so the mesh counters could be read) saw no retries and no throttling at the home nodes. So the bottleneck is somewhere else. [crb-hierarchy-findings.md]

The single-writer limit sits inside the core. Part 5 of the root run (the write-path counter test) counted zero L1 and L2 refills-for-write, zero write-backs and no crosspoint credit stalls while one writer ran.
That writer moved 69.18 to 71.34 GB/s at 8 MiB and 62.91 GB/s at 1 GiB. [crb/results/sudo-20261102T211150Z/writepath.csv best rows]
A partner on the same port raised the total to 80.62 to 82.05 GB/s, two ports to 118.85 to 122.06 GB/s, and four ports to 223.98 to 229.83 GB/s.
Core-to-slice latency ran 19 to 44 ns by distance. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, from sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv]

On Asimov, boot A counted 0.000 L2 prefetch refills (event 0x81BD) per load on fresh random chains from 1.5 to 32 MiB. It counted 0.004 to 0.029 per load at 512 KiB to 1 MiB, and 0.124 to 0.212 per load on the repeat rows at 192 to 384 KiB.
With the prefetchers off (boot B) the 24 random rows moved only -5.6 % to +5.3 %. So the C1-Nano does not learn a random chain, unlike the V3AE. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.2 and section 11.2]
The CME (the Asimov per-cluster matrix engine) does prefetch on a repeated chain: 3.12 to 17.47 prefetch refills per load from 8 to 48 KiB. [asimov-cme-run4.html, 'CME L1 refills per load' chart]
A sparse 256 KiB chain on the CRB ran 145 to 158 ns per load with 3.8 to 7.3 L2 refills per load. The dense chain ran 28.9 ns per load with 1.00 refills per load.
That is 2.8 to 6.3 extra refills per load. The CME plan carried this as a warning about the method, not as an Asimov measurement. [asimov/CME-plan.md section 11, lines 596-599]
polished.open: The CRB write collapse has no named bottleneck. A counter read at the mesh crosspoints or the memory controllers under the 32+32 writer placement would locate it. The raw CSV of the CRB sparse-chain run (145 to 158 ns per load) is not in the cache-perf tree. Those numbers rest on CME-plan.md alone.

chart.title: CRB DRAM bandwidth by thread placement across the two meshes
chart.takeaway: Splitting 64 writers 32+32 over the two meshes cuts the total from 394.15 GB/s to 172.81 GB/s. Readers split the same way keep 327.91 GB/s. Only writes collapse.

terms.definition: The Arm Phoenix reference server board, with Neoverse V3AE cores and two CMN meshes, used before and beside the Asimov runs.
Arm Neoverse V3AE, the CRB core. Its temporal prefetcher learns a repeated miss sequence and refills L2 early.
The Asimov core. Boot A and boot B showed it does not learn a random chain.
The Asimov per-cluster matrix engine. It does prefetch on a repeated chain.
A list of pointers in memory walked one load at a time, so each load waits for the previous one.
A chain walked more than once, so a prefetcher can learn the order and fetch the lines early.
A chain the core has never walked. One pass over it gives the true miss cost.
Reporting only the fastest of N repeated walks. It hides the cost of the first touch.
One of the two dies of the CRB. Each has its own mesh.
CMN, the Arm coherent mesh network that joins cores, home nodes and memory controllers.
A mesh node that owns one slice of the SLC. Each CRB mesh has 64 of them.
System level cache, 128 MiB on the CRB, held in the mesh home nodes. sysfs lists it as L3.
The per-core second-level cache, 2 MiB on the CRB.
A cache line brought into a cache after a miss. Prefetch refills are brought in by a hardware prefetcher before any load asks for them.
The Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction. The --flush option runs it on every line before a timed pass.
The PMU (performance monitoring unit) counter for L2 refills caused by a hardware prefetcher.
A switch point of the mesh. A credit stall there means the mesh had no room to accept a request.
A core-to-mesh connection. Several cores can share one port.
The CRB run of 2026-10-30 that read the mesh counters outside the cores.
The CRB follow-up of 2026-11-02 run with root rights so the mesh counters could be read.

polished.one_line: CME hardware counters put the matrix issue rate at 69 % of its ceiling. A timer on a 4,096-FMOPA loop said 98 %.
looked_wrong: The CME ceiling is 0.5 FMOPA issues per CME cycle (one FMOPA per 2 cycles).

The hardware counters gave CME_OP_MMDP_ISSUE / CME_CYCLES = 0.3455 issues per CME cycle on all five workers. That is 69 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.3, asimov-bench dpa/stress, Spokane request 1504].
A timer gave 4,173 ns for 4,096 FMOPA (FP32, register operands) on one core, boot M2.
That is 1.019 ns per FMOPA, or 2.04 cycles per FMOPA. That is 98 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.2, asimov-bench boot M2].
Two cores of DSU0 (the first cluster of two cores) issuing 2 x 4,096 FMOPA together took 8,909 ns, boot M2. That is 1.088 ns per FMOPA.
The pair got no more total work done than one core. Each instruction was 6.7 % slower [cme-survey.html section 4.2, boot M2].
Two st1h instructions (a CME store of 16-bit elements) issued back-to-back cost 3.0 CME cycles per instruction.
The RTL (the hardware design source) reading says 1 cycle [cme-survey.html section 9, Jacob Geldbach's run 4007 on GA13, RTL a10181848].
why_wrong: Two independent methods on the same unit disagreed by 29 percentage points: 98 % by the timer and 69 % by the counters.

Arm's own half-matmul test comment says one FMOPA per 2 cycles. The llvm-mca C1-Nano model (the LLVM instruction-timing model for this core) gives FMOPA 2.00 cycles per instruction [cme-survey.html sections 2 and 4.1].

For stores, the llvm-mca C1-Nano model lists ST1B (a CME store of 8-bit elements) of 2 vectors at 1.00 cycle per instruction and of 4 vectors at 2.00 cycles, with 2 cycles of latency [cme-survey.html section 4.1].
st1h is not in that table. A 3.0-cycle store is three times the model's rate [cme-survey.html section 4.1].

tests.name: Re-balanced loop with CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES read beside the issue ratio
tests.measures: The loop was rearranged to 8 FMOPA + 8 LD1B (a CME vector load) + 12 FMLA (a vector multiply-add) per iteration, on asimov-bench dpa/stress, Spokane request 1511 (October 2026, not a membench-jibin run). It measures the MMDP issue ratio when the instruction stream does not starve the CME. It also records whether the CME stays allocated to the core for the whole window. A ratio near 0.5 would mean the 69 % came from the instruction stream, not from the CME.

tests.name: CME store rows by footprint, one thread on CPU 2
tests.measures: It runs cme-write (ST1B of four vectors, 256 B per instruction) at 16 KiB to 32 MiB. It runs cme-str16 (one 64 B vector per store) at 16 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB. Both run in run 3 (004, the L3 off) and run 6 boots F1 and F2 (011/012, the L3 on, prefetchers on then off) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 011 and 012]. It measures the sustained CME store rate in bytes per CME cycle. A rate of 0.5 stores per cycle would match the llvm-mca rate of 2.00 cycles for ST1B of four vectors. A rate of one store per 3.0 cycles would match the st1h cost.

tests.name: CME L1 write rows in the single-call form, 4 to 24 KiB
tests.measures: The single-call form runs every pass of a rep (one repetition of the kernel) inside one call. That removes the per-call cost. It measures the CME store rate in stores per cycle with the footprint inside L1 [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012].

showed: The re-balanced loop gave 0.4916 to 0.4922 issues per CME cycle. That is 98 % of the 0.5 ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511].
CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES was 0.9993, so the CME stayed allocated to the core [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511].

The bench authors attribute the original 69 % to the in-order front end: about 44 instructions per 8 FMOPA at an IPC of 1.9 in the verbatim loop [cme-survey.html section 4.3, kernels.h cme_fmopa_fit comment].
So the timer and the counters agree once the stream fits the front end.
The two-core result of 1.088 ns per FMOPA is explained by the one CME per DSU being time-shared between its two cores [cme-survey.html section 2].
cme-write in run 3 (004, the L3 off) gave 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s from 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB, best of 3 reps [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004].
That is 32 bytes per cycle at 2.003 GHz (derived), or 0.5 of a 64 B store per cycle. This matches the llvm-mca rate of 2.00 cycles for ST1B of four vectors [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1].

cme-write in run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on) gave 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB (26 bytes per cycle) and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB (20 to 21 bytes per cycle), both derived [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011].
Boot F2 (012, prefetchers off) gave 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012].
cme-str16 gave 63.7, 63.9 and 62.0 GB/s in run 3 and 52.1, 42.7 and 40.6 GB/s in boot F1 at 16 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011].

The single-call L1 write rows on boot F1 read 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB, or 0.42 of a 64 B store per cycle (derived) [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1].
polished.open: The st1h 3.0-cycle cost and the 0.5 ST1B stores per cycle stay open. No membench-jibin row uses st1h. No source on disk gives the CME store path width that would settle the ST1B rate. So both are Insufficient data [asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. The fall of cme-write from 63.7 GB/s (run 3, the L3 off) to 51.6 GB/s (boot F1, the L3 on) is a separate open item. The page's hypothesis is that the stores allocate in the L3 and drain at its rate [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

terms.definition: The Arm C1-SME2 matrix streaming unit. There is one per DSU cluster, shared by its two cores.
A cluster of two C1-Nano cores that share one CME. DSU0 is the first cluster.
The SME outer-product multiply-add instruction. The CME can issue at most one every 2 cycles (the half-matmul rate, a ceiling of 0.5 issues per cycle).
The hardware counter CME_OP_MMDP_ISSUE divided by CME_CYCLES. It counts matrix instructions issued per CME cycle.
The fraction of core cycles in which the CME was allocated to that core. A value near 1.0 means the core held the CME for the whole window.
The C1-Nano issues instructions strictly in program order. A long stream of non-CME instructions between FMOPA delays the next FMOPA.
Instructions per cycle, how many instructions the core completes per clock cycle on average.
CME instructions: st1h stores 16-bit elements, ST1B stores 8-bit elements (2 or 4 vectors per instruction), LD1B loads a vector, FMLA is a vector multiply-add.
The LLVM instruction-timing model for this core. It lists cycles per instruction and latency for each instruction.
The hardware design source (register-transfer level). A reading of the RTL gives the designed timing.

A separate benchmark suite from another team. Its boots M2 and M3 gave the timer rows, and its dpa/stress runs on Palladium (an emulation platform) gave the counter rows. It is not part of the membench-jibin result folders.
A test platform and run number used by Jacob Geldbach's team for the st1h measurement, on RTL a10181848.
membench-jibin store kernels run on the CME: cme-write uses ST1B of four vectors (256 B per instruction), cme-str16 stores one 64 B vector per instruction, cme-copy copies (reads and writes).
A kernel form where every pass of a rep (one repetition) runs inside one call, so the per-call setup cost is not counted.
Run 3 (004) ran with the L3 cache disabled. Run 6 boots F1 (011) and F2 (012) ran with it enabled. Boot F2 also had the hardware prefetchers off.
Gigabytes per second with GB = 1e9 bytes. Bytes per cycle is derived from it at a 2.003 GHz clock.
